nuance.etymology: From Late Latin dominicalis, from dominicus, 'of the Lord', from dominus, 'lord'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with the stress on the first syllable, as in 'DOM-ih-nih-kul'.
Confusing it with Dominican, the adjective for the Dominican Republic or the Dominican religious order.
nuance.biblical_note: In Christian usage the term points to Jesus as Lord and to the Lord's Day. The Greek word kyriakos means 'of the Lord', as in Revelation 1:10, where John says he was 'in the Spirit on the Lord's day' (RSV). The phrase 'the Lord's Supper' in 1 Corinthians 11:20 (RSV) uses kyriakon, showing the same root. Matthew 12:8 (RSV) says the Son of Man is lord of the sabbath, linking Jesus' authority to the day of rest.

senses.definition: Made up of two matching or complementary elements.
senses.example: The closet has double doors.

senses.definition: Of twice the quantity.
senses.example: Give me a double serving of mashed potatoes.

senses.definition: Of a family relationship, related on both the maternal and paternal sides of a family.
senses.example: He's my double cousin as my mother's sister married my father's brother.

senses.definition: Designed for two (people, cars, etc.).
senses.example: a double room

senses.definition: Folded in two; composed of two layers.
senses.example: She wrapped the sandwich in double sheets of parchment to keep it from drying out.

senses.definition: Stooping; bent over.
senses.example: The old gardener was bent double over his roses, pulling weeds all morning.

senses.definition: Having two aspects; ambiguous.
senses.example: a double meaning

senses.definition: False, deceitful, or hypocritical.
senses.example: a double life

senses.definition: Of flowers, having more than the normal number of petals.
senses.example: This variety of rose has double blossoms with many more petals than the common kind.

senses.definition: Of an instrument, sounding an octave lower.
senses.example: a double bass

senses.definition: Of time, twice as fast.
senses.example: The cartoon's clock ticks at double time, so the minutes pass twice as quickly.

senses.definition: Twice over; twofold; doubly.
senses.example: The package weighs double what the last one did, so shipping costs more.

senses.definition: Two together; two at a time.
senses.example: When I met the twins, I thought I was seeing double.

senses.definition: Into two halves or sections.
senses.example: The old man was bent double under his heavy burden.

senses.definition: Twice the number, amount, size, etc.
senses.example: I did double his sales this month.

senses.definition: A person who resembles and stands in for another person, often for safety purposes.
senses.example: Saddam Hussein was rumored to have many doubles.

senses.definition: A drink with two portions of alcohol.
senses.example: On second thought, make that a double.

senses.definition: Two shifts of work back to back.
senses.example: I work a double this weekend.

senses.definition: A ghostly apparition of a living person; a doppelgänger.
senses.example: Some villagers swore they had seen her double walking through the orchard at midnight.

senses.definition: A sharp turn, especially a return on one's own tracks.
senses.example: The fox made a double back through the creek to lose the hounds.

senses.definition: A redundant item for which an identical item already exists.
senses.example: I have more than 200 stamps in my collection but they're not all unique: some are doubles.

senses.definition: A call that increases certain scoring points if the last preceding bid becomes the contract.
senses.example: She made the double, hoping her partner would bid again and raise the stakes.

senses.definition: A strike in which the object ball is struck so as to make it rebound against the cushion to an opposite pocket.
senses.example: He played a double off the cushion and sank the eight ball in the corner pocket.

senses.definition: A bet on two horses in different races in which any winnings from the first race are placed on the horse in the later race.
senses.example: He placed a double on two horses, hoping the first winner would carry his winnings forward.

senses.definition: The narrow outermost ring on a dartboard.
senses.example: Aim for the double ring on the outside edge of the board to score twice the points.

senses.definition: A hit on this ring.
senses.example: Her last dart landed a double that gave her the win at the pub.

senses.definition: A tile that has the same value (i.e. the same number of pips) on both sides.
senses.example: In the game, you can play a double six on the first turn if you have it.

senses.definition: A double-precision floating-point number.
senses.example: The sine function returns a double.

senses.definition: Two competitions, usually one league and one cup, won by the same team in a single season.
senses.example: Winning the double is rare, so the club celebrated after taking both the league and cup.

senses.definition: A boat for two scullers.
senses.example: We rented a double for the lake trip and rowed it together across the calm bay.

senses.definition: A double feast.
senses.example: The monastery celebrated the feast day with a double, with extra dishes and longer prayers.

senses.definition: Synonym of double-quick (“fast marching pace”).
A double agent.
Someone who identifies with the same kintype.
Someone who yumeships with the same character as another person.
A two-base hit.
senses.example: The catcher hit a double to lead off the ninth.

senses.definition: The feat of scoring twice in one game.
The feat of winning two events in a single meet or competition.
senses.example: In 1996, Michael Johnson achieved a double by winning both the 200 and 400 meter dashes.

senses.definition: The achievement of 1000 runs and 100 wickets taken in a single season.
Playing the same part on two instruments, alternately.
A secondary instrument with which a musician is skilled.
(historical) A former French coin worth one-sixth of a sou.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) A copper coin worth one-eighth of a penny.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (dated) A double-cross or betrayal.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: To multiply by two.
senses.example: The company doubled their earnings per share over last quarter.

senses.definition: To increase by 100%, to become twice as large in size.
senses.example: Our earnings have doubled in the last year.

senses.definition: To be the double of; to exceed by twofold; to contain or be worth twice as much as.
To fold over so as to make two folds.
senses.example: To make a pleat, double the material at the waist.

senses.definition: To clench (a fist).
To join or couple.
To repeat exactly; copy.
To serve a second role or have a second purpose. [with as]
senses.example: A spork is a kind of fork that doubles as a spoon.

senses.definition: To act as substitute for (another theatrical performer in a certain role, etc).
To play (both one part and another, in the same play, etc).
To turn sharply, following a winding course.
To make a call that will double certain scoring points if the preceding bid becomes the contract.
To double down.
To cause (a ball) to rebound from a cushion before entering the pocket.
To go or march at twice the normal speed.
To multiply the strength or effect of by two.
senses.example: Sorry, this store does not double coupons.

senses.definition: To transmit simultaneously on the same channel as another station, either unintentionally or deliberately, causing interference.
senses.example: Could you please repeat your last transmission? Another station was doubling with you.

senses.definition: To operate as a double agent.
To get a two-base hit.
senses.example: The batter doubled into the corner.

senses.definition: To sail around (a headland or other point).
To duplicate (a part) either in unison or at the octave above or below it.
To be capable of performing (upon an additional instrument).
To unite, as ranks or files, so as to form one from each two.

core.definition: Twice as much or as many; made up of two matching or complementary parts.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable, and the vowel is the short uh of 'cup'. The second syllable is a syllabic l with no extra vowel, so it sounds like 'DUH-buhl', not 'duh-BELL'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: a basic word for quantity, matching pairs or doubling.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use double constantly in everyday speech, such as a double cheeseburger, a double espresso or double-checking something. In bars, 'a double' means twice the normal shot of liquor. It is not mainly British, and it works as an adjective, adverb, noun and verb.

distinctions.note: Twice is an adverb meaning two times, as in 'twice as many'; double works as adjective, noun and verb too.
Dual means having two distinct functions or parts, while double means twice the quantity or a matching pair.
A duplicate is an exact copy; a double is something present twice in quantity or a lookalike.

examples.everyday: I'll have a double espresso, please, because I didn't sleep well last night.
examples.professional: Let's double the test coverage before the release, since the last bug slipped through.
examples.analytical: If the sample size doubles, the standard error shrinks by a factor of about 0.7, not by half.

nuance.analogy: Double is like pouring a second shot of the same drink into the same glass: one more of exactly the same thing.
nuance.etymology: From Old French doble, from Latin duplus, 'twofold'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'double than' instead of 'twice as many as' or 'double as many as'
Using 'a double' for food in a restaurant, where it may sound like you asked for a double drink
Mispronouncing the second syllable as 'bull' instead of a soft buhl

double.etymology: From Middle English *double*, from Old French *doble*, *double*, from Latin *duplus* (“twofold”).

senses.definition: Synonym of dragon (“a type of musket with a short, large-caliber barrel and a flared muzzle, metaphorically exhaling fire like a mythical dragon”).
senses.example: The museum displays a brass dragoon with a flared muzzle from the 1700s.

senses.definition: A man with a fierce or unrefined manner, like a dragoon (noun sense 1.2).
senses.example: My grandfather was a dragoon at the family dinner table, barking orders at everyone.

senses.definition: A variety of pigeon, originally a cross between a horseman and a tumbler.
senses.example: Our county fair judge awarded first prize to a dragoon pigeon with striking plumage.

senses.definition: (historical) Originally, a soldier armed with a dragoon musket (noun sense 1.1) who fought both on foot and mounted on a horse; now, a cavalier or horse soldier from a regiment formerly armed with such muskets.
senses.example: The dragoon regiment rode across the frontier in 1758 to protect the trading posts.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: Chiefly followed by into: to force (someone) into doing something through harassment and intimidation; to coerce.

(historical) To subject (a Huguenot) to the dragonnades (“a policy instituted by Louis XIV of France in 1681 to intimidate Protestant Huguenots to convert to Roman Catholicism by billeting dragoons (noun sense 1.2) in their homes to abuse them and destroy or steal their possessions”).
senses.example: Royal troops were ordered to dragoon the Huguenot families of the province in 1685.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) To cause (someone) to be attacked by dragoons.
senses.example: The king's ministers chose to dragoon the rebellious villagers rather than negotiate.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: To force someone into doing something through pressure, threats or intimidation; to coerce or bully them into it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable: druh-GOON. The first syllable is a reduced 'uh.' The final syllable rhymes with 'moon,' not 'gone' or 'goo-nin.'

nuance.connotation: Negative; it implies pressure, force and a loss of freedom of choice.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, 'dragoon' is mostly used in writing, news analysis or literary prose, often with 'into' as in 'dragooned into.' In everyday conversation people say 'roped into' or 'pressured into.' Historically, dragoons were mounted soldiers, and under Louis XIV French dragoons were billeted on Huguenot families to pressure them to convert.

distinctions.note: Coerce is more formal and general, and can refer to legal or political force; dragoon usually suggests a person being pushed around by a more forceful individual or group.
Pressure is a common, milder word for persuasion that becomes uncomfortable; dragoon is stronger and implies the person has little real choice.

examples.everyday: My cousin dragooned me into driving her to the airport at five in the morning.
examples.professional: The project lead dragooned two analysts into rewriting the report before the board meeting, even though they had other deadlines.
examples.analytical: A state that dragoons its citizens into faith has confused compliance with conviction, and a faith forced in this way is no faith at all.

nuance.analogy: Like a soldier billeted in your house, dragoon pressure arrives uninvited and stays until you give in.
nuance.etymology: From French dragon, the name for a short musket and for a mounted soldier armed with one; the word is linked to the image of a fire-breathing dragon.
common_mistakes: Using 'dragoon' as a harmless synonym for 'invite'; it always implies force or pressure.
Saying 'dragoon to do' instead of 'dragoon someone into doing'; the preposition 'into' is needed.

senses.definition: Drive someone to a place and leave them there.
senses.example: Can you drop me off at the airport on your way to work?

core.definition: To drive someone to a place and leave them there.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on OFF, and someone is weakly stressed on SUM with an unstressed wun. Don't stress the second syllable of someone.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical; it describes giving someone a ride.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use drop someone off for giving someone a ride to a place, as in Can you drop me off at the airport? The person is the object and goes between drop and off. It is the everyday verb for offering a ride. A simple Thanks for the ride is a natural reply, and no formal response is needed.

distinctions.note: Pick up is the opposite: collecting someone from a place.
Take is more general and can mean bring someone along; drop someone off implies leaving them at the destination.

collocations: drop someone off at the airport

examples.everyday: Can you drop me off at the corner? I'll walk the rest of the way.
examples.professional: I'll drop the client off at the conference center before heading to the office.
examples.analytical: Parents who drop their children off at school every morning are performing a daily ritual of trust.

nuance.analogy: It is like delivering a package to a doorstep, except the package is a person.
nuance.etymology: From drop, meaning to let fall or set down, plus off, meaning away from a place.
common_mistakes: Placing the pronoun after off; say drop me off, not drop off me.
Saying drop her off to downtown; the correct preposition is at or downtown without to.

conversation.text: I'll drop you off at the front door and go park.
Can you drop me off at the station on your way?
He dropped his daughter off at school before work.

senses.definition: Synonym of pharmacy, especially a small standalone general store which includes a pharmacy.
senses.example: I picked up my prescription at the drugstore on the corner before heading home.

core.definition: A store, usually in a shopping area, that sells medicine and also sells everyday items such as snacks, cosmetics, and cards.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the first syllable, and the second part is a light secondary stress. The r in "store" is pronounced clearly, as in most American words.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a friendly, everyday word for a familiar neighborhood store.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use drugstore for a neighborhood store that sells prescriptions and household goods, such as CVS or Walgreens. The word pharmacy usually refers to the counter where prescriptions are filled, and people often say "I'm going to the drugstore" for any trip to buy shampoo or medicine. The British equivalent is chemist's.

distinctions.note: A pharmacy is the part of the store that fills prescriptions, while a drugstore is the whole store with many items.
A grocery store mainly sells food, while a drugstore mainly sells medicine and personal care items.

examples.everyday: Can you stop at the drugstore on your way home and pick up some cough syrup?
examples.professional: Our team tested the new prescription app with the pharmacists at the local drugstore chain.
examples.analytical: The rise of the drugstore in twentieth-century America changed how people shopped for health and convenience.

nuance.analogy: A drugstore is like a small town crossroads where medicine, snacks, and greeting cards all share one set of shelves.
nuance.etymology: Compound of drug and store; the -store element is from Old French estorer, to furnish.
common_mistakes: Saying "chemist" in American conversation, which sounds British.
Using drugstore to mean illegal drugs, when it refers only to a store.

conversation.text: I'm stopping at the drugstore to get some sunscreen and shampoo.
Is there a drugstore that's open late around here?
The drugstore has a sale on vitamins this week.

senses.definition: A type of random walk in which termination conditions lead to a biased ending state.
senses.example: Her model of stock prices behaved like a drunkard's walk, drifting toward a biased endpoint.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see drunkard,‎ 's,‎ walk: how a drunk person ambulates.
senses.example: After the party, he staggered home in a drunkard's walk, weaving from curb to curb.

core.definition: In statistics, a random walk in which each step goes in a random direction, so the path has no planned course.

pronunciation.tip: Stress DRUNG-kerdz on the first syllable, and reduce the ard to a light rhotic schwa. Most Americans say walk with an aw sound, so it rhymes with talk.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In statistics it is a neutral model term; in everyday speech it is a mildly humorous description.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday speech, 'drunkard's walk' can describe a staggering, zigzag walk, but it is mainly a technical term in statistics and probability. Data scientists and teachers use it because it gives a memorable image of random motion. Most people in data work just say 'random walk', and this name is used mostly in lectures and textbooks.

distinctions.note: Drunkard's walk is a playful name for the standard random walk model, so the two terms describe the same idea.
A biased walk favors some directions over others, while a drunkard's walk has no preferred direction.

examples.everyday: He came out of the bar on a drunkard's walk, weaving from one side of the sidewalk to the other.
examples.professional: In the simulation, each particle follows a drunkard's walk, so its expected distance from the start grows with the square root of the number of steps.
examples.analytical: The drunkard's walk offers a clean model of diffusion, showing how pure randomness can spread a system through space over time.

nuance.analogy: Like a stumbler in the dark, each step picks a random direction, so the path wanders with no plan.
common_mistakes: Thinking it refers only to a real drunk person's walk; in statistics it is a random-walk model.
Stressing the second syllable of drunkard; the stress is on DRUNG.

senses.definition: A pang or expression of doubt.
senses.example: A quiet dubitation crossed his mind as he read the surprising test results again.

core.definition: A brief moment or flicker of doubt, hesitation, or uncertainty about a belief or decision.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the TAY syllable, with a lighter secondary stress on doo. The -tion ending is pronounced shun, and the middle vowels are reduced to a quick ih.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It describes an inner hesitation, often one the speaker wishes to dismiss.
nuance.usage_note: 'Dubitation' is rare in American speech and mostly found in older or literary writing. Americans say 'doubt,' 'hesitation,' or 'second thoughts' instead. If you use it, it will sound deliberate and bookish, so it works best in written reflection or formal prose.

distinctions.note: 'Doubt' is the general, everyday word; 'dubitation' emphasizes a brief, passing pang rather than a settled state.
'Hesitation' is a pause before acting; 'dubitation' is the inner uncertainty that causes the pause.

examples.professional: Even after the test results came in, the lead engineer voiced a flicker of dubitation before signing off.
examples.analytical: The author admits a momentary dubitation about the doctrine, yet returns at once to the confidence of faith.

nuance.analogy: Like a small stone in your shoe: noticeable for a moment, but easy to ignore.
nuance.etymology: From Latin dubitatio, from dubitare 'to doubt.'
common_mistakes: Misspelling it as 'dubitation' with 'dubbing' in mind; the root is doubt, not dub.
Using it in casual speech, where 'doubt' or 'second thoughts' sounds more natural.
nuance.biblical_note: 'Dubitation' is not a Scripture word, but the New Testament treats doubt seriously. The Greek word distazō means to waver or doubt, and Matthew describes Peter beginning to sink when he doubts on the water (Matthew 14:31). Matthew 28:17 says some of the disciples doubted even after meeting the risen Christ. Matthew 21:21 describes faith that does not doubt, contrasting it with a divided mind.

dubitation.etymology: From Late Middle English *dubytacion*, from Middle French *dubitation*, from Latin *dubitātiō*.

senses.definition: A stupid person; a fool.

core.definition: A person who is slow-witted or stupid, especially one who is also boring; a fool.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The second syllable is a reduced, r-colored vowel, so the word ends in 'erd', not 'yard'.

nuance.connotation: Negative and insulting; it is harsh and somewhat old-fashioned.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dullard mostly in writing, in book reviews, opinion columns, and satire. In speech, people more often say 'bozo', 'dope', 'knucklehead', or 'dunce'. Calling someone a dullard is rude, and it is best reserved for describing a character or a public figure.

distinctions.note: A dunce is a student who is bad at learning; 'dullard' is broader and describes a person who lacks wit and interest.
A fool acts foolishly or is easily deceived; a dullard is someone whose mind is slow and uninspired.
'Bozo' is a very informal, mildly comic insult for a foolish person; 'dullard' is more literary and more cutting.

examples.everyday: Don't be a dullard about it; come out with us tonight and have some fun.
examples.professional: Stop calling the vendor a dullard; he simply didn't read the spec, and we can fix that with a short call.
examples.analytical: Victorian satire often casts the bureaucrat as a dullard, a figure of mechanical stupidity and self-importance.

nuance.analogy: A dull blade of a mind that never cuts through anything.
nuance.etymology: From dull plus the suffix -ard, a suffix used for persons, as in coward.
common_mistakes: Using dullard for a boring event or object; it describes a person.
Mispronouncing the last syllable as 'yard'.
Spelling it 'dulard', which drops a letter.

senses.definition: The organ of hearing, consisting of the pinna or auricle, auditory canal, eardrum, malleus, incus, stapes and cochlea.
The external part of the organ of hearing, the auricle.
A police informant.
The sense of hearing; the perception of sounds; skill or good taste in listening to music.
senses.example: a good ear for music

senses.definition: The privilege of being kindly heard; favor; attention.

That which resembles in shape or position the ear of an animal; a prominence or projection on an object, usually for support or attachment; a lug; a handle; a foot-rest or step of a spade or a similar digging tool.
senses.example: the ears of a tub, skillet, or dish; The ears of a boat are outside kneepieces near the bow.

senses.definition: A space to the left or right of a publication's front-page title, used for advertising, weather, etc.
A curled ridge in the crust of a loaf of bread where the dough was slashed before going into the oven and expands during baking.
The outer panels or flaps (protrusions) of a diaper upon which the fasteners are located, which are fastened around the wearer's waist.
A path whose endpoints may coincide but in which otherwise there are no repetitions of vertices or edges.
The fruiting body of a grain plant.
senses.example: He is in the fields, harvesting ears of corn.

senses.definition: An acroterium.
A crossette.
To take in with the ears; to hear.
To hold by the ears.
To put forth ears in growing; to form ears, as grain does.
senses.example: This corn ears well.

senses.definition: To plow.

core.definition: The organ on each side of the head that you use to hear sounds, or the visible outer part of it.

pronunciation.tip: It is a single syllable with an r-colored vowel: the r is pronounced clearly, so it sounds like 'eer'. Do not add a second syllable, and do not confuse it with 'hear' or 'year'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it is a basic body-part word, but idioms like 'all ears' and 'an ear for music' are positive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say ear for the outer part and inside of the organ of hearing. Idioms are very common: 'an ear for languages' means a natural talent for them, 'keep your ear to the ground' means stay informed, and 'I'm all ears' means I am listening closely. The police-informant sense is informal and dated.

distinctions.note: Ear is the body part. Hear is the verb for perceiving sound with the ears.
Earlobe is the soft, fleshy bottom part of the ear. Ear refers to the whole organ or its outer visible part.

examples.everyday: My ear hurts when I fly, so I chew gum during the landing.
examples.professional: The audio engineer adjusted the mix until it sounded right to a trained ear.
examples.analytical: Scripture repeatedly speaks of ears that must be opened to hear God's word, which implies that hearing is itself a spiritual act.

nuance.analogy: The ear works like a microphone that turns sound waves into signals the brain can understand.
nuance.etymology: From Old English ēare, of Germanic origin.
common_mistakes: Confusing ear with hear, which is pronounced the same way in some accents but has a different meaning.
Pronouncing the final r as a separate syllable, as in 'ee-ah'.
Using ear for an earlobe in medical writing where the proper term is auricle or pinna.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word ʾozen (אֹזֶן) means ear, and the Greek word ous (οὖς) means the same thing in the New Testament. In Scripture, the ear stands for willingness to listen to God, while a deaf or closed ear stands for refusal. Matthew 11:15 says that whoever has ears to hear should hear, a call to spiritual attention. Mark 4:9 repeats this saying in the parable of the sower. Psalm 40:6 speaks of God having given the psalmist an open ear, a sign of readiness to obey.

ear.etymology: From Middle English *eare*, *eere*, *ere*, *eyr*, *ire*, *yere*, *ȝhere*, from Old English *ēare* (“ear”), from **auʀā*, from the voiced Verner alternant of Proto-Germanic **ausô* (“ear”), from Proto-Indo-European **h₂ṓws* (“ear”), from **h₂ew-* (“to…

senses.definition: To be pregnant.

core.definition: An informal way to say that someone is pregnant, often used jokingly to excuse eating more.

pronunciation.tip: Stress TOO, the word 'two', which carries the main stress, while 'for' is reduced to a weak fer sound in fast speech. The t in 'eating' is often a quick flap that sounds like a soft d between vowels.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to lighthearted. It is playful, but it can sound dismissive or intrusive if used about someone else's eating or body.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase as a joke to justify a second dessert or a big lunch, or as a cute way to announce a pregnancy. Do not say it to a pregnant woman about her food choices or weight, because that can feel rude. A natural reply to the announcement is 'Congratulations! When are you due?'

distinctions.note: Pregnant is the plain, neutral term, while eating for two is informal and playful.
Expecting is a polite, common way to announce a pregnancy, and it is more suitable in formal or professional settings.

collocations: eating for two and loving it
eating for two at the buffet

examples.everyday: Don't judge me for the second slice of pizza, I'm eating for two these days.
examples.professional: I'm eating for two these days, so please keep the Friday meeting short because I'll need a snack.
examples.analytical: Medical advice on 'eating for two' is often misread, since pregnancy usually requires only a modest increase in daily calories.

nuance.analogy: Like a joke that hides a real milestone, making a serious change sound light and easy.
common_mistakes: Using the phrase to comment on a pregnant person's weight or food choices, which can sound rude.
Thinking the phrase means eating twice as much, when it is a joke and not a literal nutritional rule.

senses.definition: A dummy or other crude representation of a person, group or object that is hated.
senses.example: In England on Bonfire Night, an effigy is often burned.

senses.definition: A likeness of a person.
senses.example: tomb effigy

core.definition: A crude dummy or figure of a person, often burned or hanged to show anger or contempt toward that person.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, EH. The second syllable is a reduced 'fih', and the final syllable sounds like 'jee', not 'jy'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or hostile when used for a hated person, but neutral when describing a sculpted likeness.
nuance.usage_note: In American news and protests, effigies are often burned at rallies, and the phrase 'hanged in effigy' describes a symbolic public condemnation. Americans also use the word for a figure in a museum or a statue, but that use is less common in everyday speech. The word is rarely used casually for ordinary objects.

distinctions.note: A statue is usually a sculpted artwork honoring someone, while an effigy is often a crude dummy meant to show hatred or mockery.
Figure is the general word for a shape or representation; effigy specifically implies a symbolic likeness of a person.

examples.everyday: The protesters burned an effigy of the mayor outside city hall.
examples.professional: Our communications team warned that posting an effigy of the CEO in the company newsletter would look like a serious provocation.
examples.analytical: Medieval rulers were sometimes hanged in effigy when they were absent, turning a symbolic punishment into a public declaration of legitimacy.

nuance.analogy: An effigy is like a voodoo doll made to express anger publicly rather than privately.
nuance.etymology: From Latin effigies, likeness or image, from effingere, to form or shape.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable as 'ih-FIJ-ee'; the stress is on the first syllable.
Using effigy for any statue; it usually implies a crude or symbolic representation.

effigy.etymology: From French *effigie*, from Latin *effigiēs* (“likeness, effigy”), from *effingō* (“represent, portray”).

senses.definition: Someone who specializes in electrical engineering.
senses.example: Our company hired an electrical engineer to redesign the wiring in the new warehouse.

core.definition: A person who designs, develops, or tests electrical systems, equipment, circuits, or power systems.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the last syllable, neer, and the -eer is a clear r-colored vowel. The middle syllable of engineer is reduced, so say en-juh-NEER rather than EN-jin-eer.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and professional, with a sense of technical expertise.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say electrical engineer for a professional who designs power systems or electronics, and they usually add a specialty such as power or controls when talking at work. An electrician installs and repairs wiring, and it would be a mistake to call an electrician an electrical engineer. Electrical engineers often hold a degree from an ABET-accredited program.

distinctions.note: An electrician installs, maintains, and repairs wiring, while an electrical engineer designs and analyzes electrical systems.
An electronics engineer usually focuses on circuits and devices, while an electrical engineer may also work on power grids and large systems.

examples.everyday: My brother is an electrical engineer who works on power grids, so he always explains blackouts at family dinners.
examples.professional: We need an electrical engineer to review the load calculations before the new panel goes out for bids.
examples.analytical: Electrical engineers reason in terms of circuits and signals, and their habits of abstraction have shaped how cognitive scientists describe the brain.

nuance.analogy: An electrical engineer is like an architect of the power system, drawing the plans before anyone installs a wire.
nuance.etymology: Electrical from electric, from New Latin electricus; engineer from Medieval Latin ingeniator, one who devises.
common_mistakes: Calling an electrician an electrical engineer, which mixes up the trade and the profession.
Saying electric engineer, which Americans do not use for this job.

senses.definition: Any of various green gemstones, especially a green transparent form of beryl, highly valued as a precious stone.
Emerald green, a color.
senses.example: emerald:

senses.definition: Vert, when blazoning by precious stones.
senses.example: The shield's field was emerald, with a golden lion rampant across its center.

senses.definition: Any hummingbird in the genera Chlorostilbon and Elvira; and some in the genus Amazilia.
senses.example: A tiny emerald hovered over the feeder, its metallic green back flashing in the sunlight.

senses.definition: Any of various species of dragonfly of the family Corduliidae.
senses.example: We spotted an emerald skimming across the pond at dusk, its wings catching the light.

senses.definition: Of a rich green color.
senses.example: She painted the nursery walls a soft emerald, hoping it would feel calm and fresh.

senses.definition: (poetic) To ornament with, or as if with, emeralds; to make green.
senses.example: Morning sunlight emeralded the wet fields, turning every blade of grass to shimmering green.
senses.label: poetic

core.definition: A bright green precious gemstone, a green form of beryl; also the rich green color of that stone.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, EM. The second syllable is often reduced to a quick schwa, so the word has two main syllables: EM-ruhld. Pronounce the r clearly.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests beauty, wealth, and luxury.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use emerald for both the gemstone and the color, as in 'emerald earrings' or 'emerald curtains.' In jewelry shops, the gem is often described by its cut and clarity, and it is a popular birthstone for May. As an adjective, it is common in fashion and decorating.

distinctions.note: Jade is a different green stone, usually from jadeite or nephrite; emerald is a green form of beryl.
Green is the general word for the color; emerald is a specific rich, bright green associated with the gem.

examples.everyday: She wore a silver necklace with a small emerald pendant to the party.
examples.professional: The jewelry buyer said the stone is an emerald and asked for a certificate of origin.
examples.analytical: In the Apocalypse, the rainbow around the throne is described in terms of the emerald's glow, linking divine glory to brilliant color.

nuance.analogy: An emerald is like a window of green light held in stone, glowing from within.
nuance.etymology: From Greek smaragdos, green gem, passed through Old French esmeraude.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the word with the stress on the second syllable, as 'em-RALD'.
Dropping the r, saying 'EM-uld'; the American r is clear.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word smaragdos (smaragdos, emerald or a bright green gem) appears in the Revelation to John. In Revelation 4:3 the rainbow around the throne looks like an emerald, a picture of God's splendor. In Revelation 21:19 an emerald is the fourth foundation stone of the New Jerusalem, showing the city's beauty and permanence. In Ezekiel 28:13 an emerald is among the jewels of the king of Tire, described as in Eden, a sign of lost glory.

emerald.etymology: From Middle English *emeraude*, borrowed from Old French *esmeraude*, from Vulgar Latin **smaralda*, **smaraldus*, **smaraudus*, variant of Latin *smaragdus*, from Ancient Greek *σμάραγδος*, *μάραγδος*, from a language.

senses.definition: In an emphatic manner; with emphasis.
senses.example: The leaders feel emphatically that each side must prove good faith before they'll will resume their talks.

senses.definition: Most definitely; truly.
senses.example: I emphatically disagree with your claim that the data proves anything at all.

core.definition: In a way that shows strong force or certainty, often used to make a firm answer clear.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, FAT. The ending is 'ik-lee', not 'ik-al-ly', and the first syllable is weak.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It signals clear certainty, but it can sound stiff in very casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use emphatically to answer a question firmly, as in 'Emphatically not!' It appears often in writing, news and professional speech. In casual conversation people more often say 'Definitely!' or 'No way!' for the same effect.

distinctions.note: Definitely is the everyday choice in conversation, while emphatically sounds more formal and suggests stronger, sometimes forceful, insistence.
Strongly describes degree of feeling or support, whereas emphatically describes the firm, unmistakable way something is said or stated.

examples.everyday: 'Do you want to drive?' 'Emphatically not, I'm exhausted!'
examples.professional: We emphatically recommend against shipping the model before the fairness audit is finished.
examples.analytical: The text emphatically rejects the idea that reason alone can establish God's existence without revelation.

nuance.analogy: Saying something emphatically is like knocking firmly on a door instead of tapping it lightly.
nuance.etymology: From emphatic plus the adverb suffix -ally, from Greek emphatikos 'expressive'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the ending as 'ik-al-ly', with three syllables, instead of 'ik-lee'.
Using emphatically to mean 'very' or 'a lot' in everyday talk, when it actually means 'firmly and clearly'.

senses.definition: Having power to enact or establish as a law.

core.definition: Having the power to enact, or make official, a law or rule. In philosophy of mind, it describes cognition shaped by action.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first vowel-containing syllable after the prefix: NAK. The final '-ive' is a short 'iv', not 'eve'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a precise technical or legal term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: This word is rare in American speech. Legal writers usually say 'legislative' or 'enacting' instead. In philosophy and cognitive science, 'enactive' is more common, as in 'enactive approach to cognition,' describing the mind as formed through action in the world.

distinctions.note: 'Legislative' describes a body or its process of making laws; 'enactive' describes the power or capacity to make something official, and is rarely used.
'Active' means doing something in general; 'enactive' is a narrow term tied to making a law official or to a theory of mind based on action.

examples.everyday: The lawyer used a word I'd never heard, enactive, so I looked it up later.
examples.professional: Our policy memo should explain which agencies hold enactive authority under the new statute.
examples.analytical: Enactive theorists argue that the mind arises through an organism's sensorimotor engagement with its environment, not as a representation inside the head.

nuance.analogy: Like a hand that shapes clay: the shape comes from the doing, not from a plan stored somewhere in the head.
nuance.etymology: From enact plus the suffix -ive.
common_mistakes: Using 'enactive' as a synonym for 'active'
Using it in everyday speech where 'legislative' or 'enacting' is the natural word

senses.definition: A place where people or things stay temporarily.
An enclosed or fortified prehistoric site, especially a European Iron Age hill-fort.
A meeting (especially an annual meeting or important conference) of an outdoorsy group of people, such as military veterans or scouts of the scouting movement.
The act of encamping or setting up a camp; also, the state of being encamped or in a camp.
A place where people (such as displaced people, soldiers, or travelers) encamp, that is, stay in tents or other temporary structures; a camp or campsite.

core.definition: A place where people or things stay temporarily, usually a group of tents, huts, or vehicles set up outdoors.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, KAMP. The final -ment is a reduced, unstressed syllable that sounds like 'ment', not 'ment-tuh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can describe a military site, a protest camp, or a historical site, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use encampment in news reporting, about homeless encampments, protest sites, or military bases. It is more formal than 'camp' or 'campsite'. For a homeless encampment, people usually say 'homeless encampment' or simply 'the camp'. Context matters, because the word can sound sympathetic or critical.

distinctions.note: A campsite is a specific spot for camping, often in a park with facilities; an encampment is any temporary settlement, often less organized.
Camp is the everyday word; encampment sounds more formal and is common in news and history.

examples.everyday: The city cleared the encampment near the park last week, so the people moved to the shelter.
examples.professional: The disaster response team set up a temporary encampment for evacuees near the highway.
examples.analytical: The author treats the desert encampment as a symbol of the community's provisional faith.

nuance.analogy: Like a fishing village built on sand: it is there for now, but it is not meant to last forever.
nuance.etymology: From French 'encampement', from 'encamper' (to encamp), from 'camp' (field).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle as 'camp-ment' with a long a; the vowel is short, as in 'camp'.
Using encampment for a single tent; it refers to a larger group of shelters.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew behind encampment is 'machaneh' (מַחֲנֶה), meaning a camp, host, or company of people. In Genesis 32:2 Jacob calls the place Mahanaim, 'two camps', after seeing God's angels encamped around him. Numbers 2 describes the orderly encampment of the tribes of Israel around the tabernacle. These passages show encampment as both a practical arrangement and a sign of God's presence.

senses.definition: To give existence to, to produce (living creatures).
senses.example: The old tales say the gods engendered the first humans from clay.

senses.definition: To bring into existence (a situation, quality, result etc.); to give rise to, cause, create.
senses.example: Years of neglect engendered deep distrust between the tenants and the building's management.

senses.definition: To assume form; to come into existence; to be caused or produced.
senses.example: Resentment can engender quietly in a team when credit is always given to one person.

senses.definition: To endow with gender; to create gender or enhance the importance of gender.
senses.example: In many languages, articles and adjectives are engendered to agree with the noun's grammatical gender.

core.definition: To cause a feeling, situation, or problem to arise or develop; to give rise to something.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, and the first syllable sounds like 'end,' not 'in.' The final syllable is a reduced 'er' sound, so say 'JEN-der' with no separate 'd' sound after 'n.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is used for both good and bad results, such as trust or conflict. The meaning depends on the object it takes.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in writing, essays, reports, and serious discussion, not in casual speech. In conversation people usually say 'cause,' 'create,' or 'lead to' instead. It sounds natural when describing how one situation produces another, such as how a policy engenders resentment.

distinctions.note: Generate is neutral and general, often about making energy, ideas, or output, while engender usually describes producing feelings or social conditions.
Cause is common and direct, while engender is more formal and suggests a gradual process of growth or development.

examples.everyday: Her constant lateness started to engender some frustration among her teammates.
examples.professional: Our rushed rollout may engender distrust among customers if we don't explain the changes clearly.
examples.analytical: Fear of the unknown can engender a moral rigidity that suppresses honest inquiry.

nuance.analogy: Like a seed that grows into a plant, an engendered feeling grows out of the conditions around it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'ingenerare,' meaning 'to produce within,' from 'in-' and 'generare,' to beget.
common_mistakes: Using 'engender' in casual speech where 'cause' or 'create' sounds more natural.
Stressing the first syllable as in 'EN-gender' instead of 'en-JEN-der.'

engender.etymology: From Middle English *engendren*, from Old French *engendrer*, from Latin *ingenero*.

senses.definition: To inject or put venom onto or into (someone or something).
senses.example: The assassin envenomed the tip of his dagger before slipping into the crowded banquet hall.

senses.definition: To acerbate, make bitter.

core.definition: To fill something with venom or spite, or to make someone's words, feelings or actions bitter and hostile.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, VEN. The last syllable is a reduced vowel, so it sounds like 'um', not 'om'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes hostility, bitterness or harmful intent.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use envenom mostly in writing, especially literary or journalistic prose, for an argument or insult that has been made poisonous. In everyday speech they would more likely say 'make it nasty' or 'make it bitter.' It is not usually used about snakes in casual talk.

distinctions.note: Poison usually means to make someone ill or die, while envenom is figurative or literal about adding venom, often with spite.
Embitter means to make someone resentful over time, while envenom suggests a sharper, more active injection of hostility.

examples.everyday: After the fight, she tried to be polite, but her comments about his car were envenomed.
examples.professional: The meeting was calm until one manager envenomed the discussion with a personal attack on a colleague.
examples.analytical: The critic argues that rhetoric can envenom public life by turning disagreement into contempt.

nuance.analogy: Like adding a drop of poison to a glass of water: the whole drink changes.
nuance.etymology: From en- 'put into' and venom, from Old French venin, from Latin venenum, poison.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the last syllable as 'om' rather than 'um'.
Using envenom for ordinary anger; it is stronger and more literary.

envenom.etymology: From Middle English *envenymen*, from Old French *envenimer* (“to poison, taint”); equivalent to *en* + *venom*.

senses.definition: Resentful desire of something possessed by another or others (but not limited to material possessions).
senses.example: Her envy of her sister's promotion made it hard to celebrate with her.

senses.definition: An object of envious notice or feeling.
senses.example: The new convertible was the envy of everyone in the company parking lot.

senses.definition: A red-skinned variety of eating apple.
senses.example: We bought a bag of envy apples at the farmers market for the kids' lunches.

senses.definition: To feel displeasure or hatred towards (someone) for their good fortune or possessions.
senses.example: I try not to envy friends who get promotions faster than I do.

senses.definition: To resentfully or discontentedly desire (something someone else has that one lacks).
senses.example: Many kids envy their older brother's freedom to stay out late.

core.definition: A resentful wish for something another person has, such as possessions, success or good luck.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, EN. The final vowel is a clear 'ee', and the v is voiced, not like 'f'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a resentful or bitter wish for what others have.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use envy both in casual speech and in serious moral discussion. In everyday talk they often say 'I envy you' lightly and kindly. In formal or religious contexts it names a sin. A natural reply to 'I envy you' is 'Thanks, I'm lucky.'

distinctions.note: Envy is wanting what someone else has, while jealousy is fear of losing what you already have or are owed.
Covetousness is a strong desire to take what belongs to another, while envy may be resentful without a desire to take it.

examples.everyday: I have to admit I feel a little envy when you talk about your trip to Italy.
examples.professional: Some colleagues felt envy when the new manager's project received more funding.
examples.analytical: Scripture treats envy as a disordered desire that poisons the one who harbors it and wounds the community.

nuance.analogy: Like a weed in a garden: it grows quietly in the heart and spreads to everything around it.
nuance.etymology: From Old French envie, from Latin invidia, from invidere, to look at maliciously.
common_mistakes: Using envy as a verb with a preposition; say envy someone, not envy of someone.
Confusing envy with jealousy in romantic situations.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Bible envy is a serious moral fault. The Greek word is phthonos, meaning envy or ill will toward another's good, and the Hebrew idea of kin'ah, jealousy or zeal, can also carry envy in negative contexts. Mark 7:22 lists envy among evils that come from within the heart. Galatians 5:21 includes envy among the works of the flesh. Matthew 27:18 says Pilate knew the chief priests had handed Jesus over out of envy.

envy.etymology: From Middle English *envie*, from Old French *envie*, from Latin *invidia* (“envy”), from *invidere* (“to look at with malice”), from *in-* (“on, upon”) + *videre* (“to look, see”).

senses.definition: Inscriptions collectively.
The study or decipherment of inscriptions, especially of ancient ones.

core.definition: The study and decipherment of inscriptions, especially ancient ones, and the inscriptions themselves considered as a body of evidence.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PIG, and the final -y is a long 'ee' sound. Don't add an extra syllable between 'ruh' and 'fee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a scholarly term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in classics, archaeology and history. It can mean the field itself ('she studies epigraphy') or the body of inscriptions ('the epigraphy of the region'). In everyday talk, people would say 'the study of ancient writing on stone'.

distinctions.note: Paleography studies handwriting in old manuscripts; epigraphy studies inscriptions carved or cut into hard materials.
Archaeology is the broad discipline of studying the human past through material remains; epigraphy is a narrower specialty within it.

examples.everyday: I took a class on ancient history, and the professor spent a week on epigraphy, which I found surprisingly fascinating.
examples.professional: Our museum's new exhibit uses epigraphy to show how the city's laws were posted publicly.
examples.analytical: Epigraphy shows that public writing was a political act, since rulers chose what to carve and where to display it.

nuance.analogy: Like reading a city's old street signs, which tell you what its leaders wanted people to remember.
nuance.etymology: From Greek epigraphe 'inscription', from epigraphein 'to write upon', with the suffix -y.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable (ih-pig-ruh-FEE), instead of the first full vowel.
Confusing 'epigraphy' with 'epigraph', which is a quotation at the start of a book.

senses.definition: One complete presentation of the training data set to an iterative machine learning algorithm.
senses.example: The neural network was trained over 500 epochs.

senses.definition: A specific instant in time, chosen as the point of reference or zero value of a system that involves identifying instants of time.
senses.example: UNIX epoch; J2000 epoch

senses.definition: A particular period of history, or of a person's life, especially one considered noteworthy or remarkable.
senses.example: The 1960s were an epoch of rapid change in American music, fashion, and civil rights.

senses.definition: A notable event which marks the beginning of such a period.
senses.example: The invention of the transistor marked the epoch that launched the modern computing era.

senses.definition: A geochronologic unit of hundreds of thousands to millions of years; a subdivision of a period, and subdivided into ages (or sometimes subepochs).
senses.example: The Holocene epoch began roughly eleven thousand years ago, at the end of the last ice age.

senses.definition: To divide (data) into segments by time period.
senses.example: I epoched the sensor readings into hourly segments so the analysis could compare daily patterns.

core.definition: In machine learning, one complete pass of a learning algorithm through the entire training dataset. In everyday use, a noteworthy period of history.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable (EP). The second syllable is a reduced schwa, so it sounds like 'uk', not 'ock' or 'eek'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in technical use; positive or dramatic in everyday historical use.
nuance.usage_note: In data science, Americans say 'epoch' constantly when discussing training neural networks, as in 'after ten epochs'. In everyday speech it means a notable era, as in 'the epoch of the personal computer'. Context usually makes the meaning clear.

distinctions.note: An era is a broad period of time, while an epoch in everyday use is a shorter, more dramatic turning point.
A batch is a subset of data processed at once, while an epoch is one full pass through the whole dataset.

examples.everyday: The 1960s were an important epoch for American music, and everyone in my family still talks about it.
examples.professional: The model reached good accuracy after ten epochs, so we'll stop training and check the validation results.
examples.analytical: Each epoch of training passes the entire dataset through the network once, which allows the model to refine its weights gradually.

nuance.analogy: An epoch is like one full lap around a running track, after which you start over from the same starting line.
nuance.etymology: From Greek epokhē, 'a stopping point' or 'fixed point in time', from epekhein 'to stop' or 'hold upon'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a long 'ee' sound as in 'EE-pock'.
Confusing epoch with batch; an epoch covers the whole training set, while a batch is only part of it.

epoch.etymology: From Medieval Latin *epocha*, from Ancient Greek *ἐποχή* (“a check, cessation, stop, pause, epoch of a star, i.e. the point at which it seems to halt after reaching the highest, and generally the place of a star; hence, a historical epoch”), from *ἐπέχω*…

conversation.text: One epoch means the model has seen every training example once.
We trained for twenty epochs, but validation loss was flat after the eighth.
The printing press marked a new epoch in how knowledge spread.

senses.definition: Anything that escalates.
senses.example: Rising fuel prices acted as an escalator that pushed up the cost of every shipment we received.

senses.definition: A motor-driven mechanical device consisting of a continuous loop of steps that automatically conveys people from one floor to another.
senses.example: There is a plastic molly-guard covering the escalator's shutdown button to prevent little kids from pushing it and stopping the escalator.

senses.definition: An upward or progressive course.
senses.example: The company's sales followed a steady escalator upward through the entire decade of growth.

senses.definition: An escalator clause.
senses.example: They agreed to a cost-of-living escalator.

senses.definition: To move by escalator.
senses.example: We escalatored to the second floor.

core.definition: A moving staircase, a motor-driven set of steps that carries people up or down between floors.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, ES, with a lighter secondary stress on lay. The final syllable is a weak er sound, not ate, so the word ends with ter.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, everyday word for a common building feature.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use escalator for the moving staircase in malls, airports, and subways; they say take the escalator or ride the escalator. The figurative sense, anything that escalates, is less common and sounds more formal. For a stationary staircase, say stairs, and for a moving flat path, say moving walkway.

distinctions.note: An elevator is an enclosed car that moves vertically, while an escalator is a continuous set of steps that you walk onto.
Stairs are fixed steps you climb yourself, while an escalator moves the steps so you can ride without effort.
A moving walkway is a flat or slightly sloped belt, while an escalator has steps and moves up or down between floors.

examples.everyday: Take the escalator up to the food court, because the elevator is out again.
examples.professional: Facilities needs to inspect the escalator before the trade show, since it carries most of the foot traffic.
examples.analytical: Transit planners treat the escalator as a flow system, measured by how many people it can move through a station each minute.

nuance.analogy: An escalator is like a staircase that does the climbing for you, step by step, without asking you to lift your legs.
nuance.etymology: Coined as a trademark around 1900, from escalade, a scaling ladder, and elevator; the root comes from Latin scala, meaning ladder.
common_mistakes: Saying the stress on the final syllable; the stress falls on the first syllable.
Pronouncing the last syllable as ate; it is a weak er sound.
Using escalator for a stationary staircase; Americans say stairs for those.

escalator.etymology: By genericization from the former trademark Escalator, created by American inventor Charles Seeberger in 1900, from Latin *ex-* (“, out of”) + *scala* (“ladder”) + *-tor*, which forms nouns of agency; see the appendix.

senses.definition: A betrothal.
senses.example: The couple's espousal was announced in the village paper last spring.

senses.definition: A wedding ceremony.
senses.example: Guests traveled for three days to attend the espousal in the old stone chapel.

senses.definition: Adoption of a plan, cause, or idea.

core.definition: Public support for or adoption of a cause, plan, belief, or idea that one commits to.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, SPOW. The final syllable is a reduced zul with a syllabic l, so do not add an extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive to neutral. It suggests sincere commitment to an ideal or position.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use espousal in formal writing, political commentary, and academic discussion to describe committed support for an idea or movement. It is rarely used in casual speech; people more often say 'support' or 'backing.' The sense of betrothal or wedding is archaic and sounds old-fashioned today.

distinctions.note: Support is common and general, while espousal implies a deliberate, public commitment to a particular cause or belief.
Advocacy is active promotion of a cause, while espousal focuses on the act of taking up the position itself.

examples.everyday: Her espousal of local parks at the city meeting surprised everyone, since she usually stays quiet.
examples.professional: The manager's espousal of agile methods helped the team move away from long release cycles.
examples.analytical: Her espousal of a liberal interpretation of the covenant raises questions about how individual conscience relates to communal tradition.

nuance.analogy: Like planting a flag in a field you intend to defend, not just walking past it.
nuance.etymology: From espouse, from Old French espouser, from Latin sponsare, 'to betroth', from spondere, 'to promise'.
common_mistakes: Using espousal for a casual opinion; it sounds too formal.
Using the archaic meaning of betrothal in modern speech without context.

espousal.etymology: From Middle English *espousal*, *espousaille*, from Old French *espousailles*, from Latin *sponsalia* (“a betrothal”), neuter plural of *sponsalis*, from *spōnsus* (“one betrothed, a spouse”); see *spouse*.

senses.definition: The view that objects have properties that are essential to them.
The theory that human beings are by nature (i.e. essentially) good and that evil is the product of society.
senses.example: Her seminar paper defended a strong essentialism about human goodness that many classmates found naive.

senses.definition: The view that all members of certain groups of people (such as those with the same race, gender, age, or sexual orientation) have common, essential traits inherent to the defining feature of the group; behavior or statement(s) that reflect such a view.
senses.example: Critics said the textbook's essentialism reduced entire ethnic groups to a handful of fixed traits.

senses.definition: The doctrine that there are certain traditional concepts, values, and skills that are essential to society and should be taught to all students.
senses.example: The school board adopted essentialism, requiring classic texts and civics skills for every student.

senses.definition: A lifestyle that seeks to minimize nonessentials in order to focus on what is important.
senses.example: Her new essentialism meant owning only a capsule wardrobe, one bag, and a few well-used books.

core.definition: The view that things, or groups of people, have fixed essential properties that define what they are.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, SEN, and reduce the first and last syllables. The -tial part is pronounced sh, so say it as shuh-liz-um rather than tee-al.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in philosophy, but often negative in social debates, where it can suggest stereotyping or fixed group traits.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use essentialism mainly in philosophy, sociology, gender studies, and debates about identity and biology. Outside academic contexts, it may sound like jargon. When used about groups, it often carries a critical tone, so be careful about how you use it in conversation.

distinctions.note: Essence is the fundamental nature of a thing. Essentialism is the theory that things have such natures, and that these natures are fixed.
Social constructionism holds that many categories are shaped by society and culture. Essentialism holds that some properties are fixed by nature.

examples.everyday: My roommate said that assuming all people from one place are alike is a form of essentialism, and I didn't know what she meant.
examples.professional: Our research team is careful to avoid essentialism when we describe demographic groups in the report.
examples.analytical: Plato's theory of Forms is a classic example of essentialism, since it posits fixed essences that make particulars what they are.

nuance.analogy: Essentialism is like believing a cup is a cup because it has a fixed cup-nature, regardless of how it was made or used.
nuance.etymology: From essential, from Latin essentialis, plus the suffix -ism.
common_mistakes: Confusing essentialism with essential, which means necessary or basic.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in es-sen-TIAL-ism.
Using it to mean essential oils or the essence of a product.

senses.definition: An advocate of essentialism.
Of or pertaining to essentialism.
senses.example: The essentialist view of gender assumes that certain traits are fixed by nature.

core.definition: A person who holds that things, or groups of people, have a fixed essence that defines what they really are.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SEN, the second syllable. The tial sounds like shuh, and the final ist is short, like list.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in philosophy, but often critical in debate, because calling someone an essentialist can suggest they oversimplify groups or people.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in philosophy classes, sociology and debates about identity, gender and race, so it is mostly academic or political. Calling someone an essentialist is a sharp criticism in some circles, so use it carefully. A more neutral way to say it is 'She holds an essentialist view of human nature.'

distinctions.note: A constructivist holds that categories such as gender are shaped by social processes, while an essentialist holds that they reflect a fixed underlying nature.
A nominalist holds that general categories are only names with no real shared essence, which is the opposite of the essentialist position.

examples.everyday: He's such an essentialist; he thinks people can't really change.
examples.professional: Our data team should avoid essentialist labels when we describe customer segments.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that Aristotle's theory of natural kinds makes him an essentialist about biological species.

nuance.analogy: An essentialist is like someone who believes a cat has a hidden catness that makes it a cat, regardless of its color or history.
nuance.etymology: From essentialism, from essential, from Latin essentia ('being').
common_mistakes: Confusing essentialist with essential, the adjective meaning necessary or important.
Stressing the wrong syllable as 'ess-en-TI-al-ist'; the main stress is on SEN.

senses.definition: The act of estranging; the act of alienating; alienation.
senses.example: Years of silence and unpaid debts caused a painful estrangement between my brother and our father.

senses.definition: The state of being alien; foreign, non-native.

core.definition: The state of being emotionally distant or cut off from someone who was once close, often because of conflict or betrayal.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable of 'estrangement,' and reduce the final syllables to a quick 'munt.' The 'g' in the root is a 'j' sound, not a hard 'g.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a painful break in a relationship, usually with some sadness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'estrangement' in formal writing, news stories, and serious personal conversations, such as talking about a family split. In everyday speech they more often say 'falling out' or 'not speaking,' so 'estrangement' sounds weighty. It is most natural in phrases like 'a period of estrangement' or 'years of estrangement.'

distinctions.note: 'Separation' can be physical or legal; 'estrangement' is emotional distance between people, even if they live together.
'Alienation' often describes a general feeling of being disconnected from society or work, while 'estrangement' describes a personal break with someone close.

examples.everyday: After years of estrangement, my cousin and I finally started talking again at the wedding.
examples.professional: The team lead's estrangement from the engineering group made the handoff difficult, so we scheduled a neutral meeting.
examples.analytical: Marx treats the worker's estrangement from the product of labor as a central feature of capitalist alienation.

nuance.analogy: Estrangement is like a garden left unwatered for years: the plants are still there, but they have grown distant and wild, and reconnecting takes patient work.
nuance.etymology: From 'estrange' with the noun suffix '-ment,' from Old French estranger, from Latin extraneus, 'foreign.'
common_mistakes: Using 'estrangement' as a general word for distance or difference between places or things.
Pronouncing the middle as 'strange-ment' with a hard 'g,' rather than the American 'j' sound.

senses.definition: To cut into a surface with an acid or other corrosive substance in order to make a pattern. Best known as a technique for creating printing plates, but also used for decoration on metal, and, in modern industry, to make circuit boards.
senses.example: The jeweler used acid to etch a delicate floral pattern into the silver band.

senses.definition: To engrave a surface.
To make a lasting impression.
senses.example: The memory of 9/11 is etched into my mind.

senses.definition: To sketch; to delineate.
senses.example: In the margin, she etched a quick outline of the bridge with her pencil.

core.definition: To cut or mark lines or a design into a hard surface, such as metal or glass, by using acid or another corrosive substance.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable, rhyming with 'fetch' and 'sketch.' Do not add a vowel before the 'tch' sound, and do not pronounce the 'e' as a long 'ee.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise craft or industrial term, and it is positive when used of art.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use etch for decorative glass or metal work, printmaking, and manufacturing, such as making circuit boards. It is also used figuratively, as in 'etched in my memory,' which is common in everyday speech and writing.

distinctions.note: Engraving cuts a surface with a sharp tool by hand, while etching uses acid to eat away the exposed parts.
Carving removes material with a blade or chisel, usually from wood or stone; etching makes fine lines with chemical action.

examples.everyday: My sister had our initials etched into the wine glasses for our wedding.
examples.professional: The fab team uses a plasma process to etch the fine traces on the wafer.
examples.analytical: Her grief etched certain images into her mind so deeply that she could not forget them.

nuance.analogy: Like a slow, patient eraser that eats away only the lines left uncovered by a protective layer.
nuance.etymology: From Dutch etsen, from German ätzen, 'to corrode' or 'to cause to eat,' related to Old High German ezzan, 'to eat.'
common_mistakes: Confusing etch with 'sketch' or 'catch' in spelling; the word ends in -tch.
Using etch for any kind of cutting, when it specifically means cutting with acid or a corrosive.

etch.etymology: From Dutch *etsen* (“to etch”), from German *ätzen* (“to etch”), from Old High German *azzon* (“to cause to bite or feed”), from Proto-Germanic **atjaną*, causative of **etaną* (“to eat”) (whence also English *eat*).

senses.definition: One who is examined, e.g. for medical reasons.
senses.example: Each examinee was asked to fast for twelve hours before the blood test.

senses.definition: One who sits an examination.

core.definition: A person who takes an examination or is examined, for example by a doctor or a testing board.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the last syllable, NEE, and the middle vowels are reduced to a quick 'uh'. Avoid stressing the first syllable, which is a common mistake for learners.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and impersonal. It sounds official.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use examinee mainly in formal, official or technical settings, such as testing agencies, professional licensing and medical forms. In everyday talk, people say 'test taker' or simply 'someone taking the test.' In medical contexts, 'patient' is more common than 'examinee'.

distinctions.note: Test taker is the common American term in everyday talk; examinee is more formal and used in official documents.
Candidate often refers to someone applying for a job or a degree; examinee stresses being tested directly.

collocations: an examinee must bring photo ID

examples.everyday: At the clinic, the examinee filled out a short form before the doctor came in.
examples.professional: Each examinee receives a unique seat number and must show identification before entering the testing room.
examples.analytical: The study compared the reasoning of each examinee across the three question types, controlling for prior training.

nuance.analogy: Like a patient on the exam table, waiting for someone else to do the evaluating.
nuance.etymology: From examine, with the suffix -ee meaning the person who is acted upon.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (EX-am-in-ee) rather than the last.
Using 'examinee' in casual speech where 'test taker' or 'patient' is more natural.

senses.definition: A brief recreational trip; a journey out of the usual way.
senses.example: While driving home I took an excursion and saw some deer.

senses.definition: A wandering from the main subject: a digression.
senses.example: Her story was a fascinating excursion, but it had nothing to do with the original question.

senses.definition: Temporary deviation from a regular course or pattern.
senses.example: After an unsuccessful excursion into banking, I've returned to public life.

senses.definition: An occurrence where an aircraft runs off the end or side of a runway or taxiway, usually during takeoff, landing, or taxi.
senses.example: The jet's landing gear collapsed, and the aircraft made an excursion off the runway into the grass.

senses.definition: A deviation in pitch, for example in the syllables of enthusiastic speech.
senses.example: The speaker's pitch excursion on the stressed syllable made his enthusiasm obvious.

senses.definition: The displacement of a body or a point from a mean position or neutral value, as in an oscillation.
senses.example: The pendulum's excursion from its resting position shrinks as friction slowly drains its energy.

senses.definition: An episode during which the fission rate of a supercritical system increases, peaks, and then decreases to a low value.
senses.example: Operators shut down the reactor after an excursion caused the fission rate to spike unexpectedly.

senses.definition: To go on a recreational trip or excursion.
senses.example: We excursioned to the lake on Saturday, packing sandwiches and a cooler.

core.definition: A short trip taken for pleasure or sightseeing, often a day outing away from home.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on -SKUR-, with the 'r' clearly pronounced as a rhotic sound. The final 'zhun' is a reduced syllable, not 'shun.'

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral, because it suggests a pleasant trip or outing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use excursion for organized day trips, such as a school excursion, a boat excursion, or a shopping excursion. In casual talk people often say 'trip' or 'outing' instead. It can also describe a digression in a speech or essay, which is more formal.

distinctions.note: Trip is the general everyday word for any journey. Excursion suggests a shorter, planned outing, often for recreation or sightseeing.
A tour is a guided visit to a place. An excursion can be unguided and is often a short side trip.

examples.everyday: We took a quick excursion to the lake on Saturday, and the kids loved the boat ride.
examples.professional: The team planned a short excursion to the client site during the offsite week.
examples.analytical: Her excursion into moral philosophy in the second chapter pulls the argument away from its original question.

nuance.analogy: An excursion is like a short detour on a road trip: you leave the main route for a pleasant side trip and then come back.
nuance.etymology: From Latin excursio, 'a running out,' from excurrere 'to run out.'
common_mistakes: Using it for a long, serious journey, where trip or expedition is better.
Using 'go in an excursion' instead of 'go on an excursion.'

excursion.etymology: Borrowed from Latin *excursiō* (“a running out, an inroad, invasion, a setting out, beginning of a speech”), from *excurrere* (“to run out”), from *ex* (“out”) + *currere* (“to run”).

senses.definition: A risk which could destroy or permanently damage an entity; a risk to one's existence.
senses.example: Many AI researchers consider runaway systems an existential risk that deserves serious attention.

senses.definition: A hypothetical future event which could cause human extinction or permanently and severely curtail humanity's potential.

core.definition: A threat that could destroy humanity or permanently and severely limit its future, such as an extinction-level event.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the word existential on STEN and the noun risk on RISK. In fast speech the final l of existential often blends into the next word, so it sounds like eg-zi-STEN-shuh-RISK.

nuance.connotation: Negative and serious, a term for catastrophic threats.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use existential risk mainly in AI safety, policy, and academic discussions, such as debates about advanced AI or pandemics. In everyday conversation, people more often say a threat to humanity or the end of the world, which sounds more natural. The term is used with care because it sounds dramatic.

distinctions.note: Catastrophic risk covers large-scale harm that may be recoverable; existential risk specifically means harm that could permanently end humanity or its potential.
Systemic risk refers to failure spreading through an interconnected system such as a bank network; existential risk refers to threats to the species or civilization as a whole.

examples.everyday: My friend who works in AI says some people think advanced systems pose an existential risk, and I didn't know what to make of that.
examples.professional: The safety review flagged the model's autonomy features as a possible contributor to existential risk, so we need a formal assessment before release.
examples.analytical: Bostrom's definition of existential risk emphasizes not only human death but the permanent loss of humanity's long-term potential.

nuance.analogy: An existential risk is like a fire that could burn down the whole house, with no way to rebuild afterward.
nuance.etymology: Existential comes from Late Latin existentialis; risk comes from Italian risco or rischio, a danger.
common_mistakes: Stressing risk on the first syllable as RIS-k instead of a single clear stress on RISK.
Using existential risk for any serious problem, when the term specifically means threats to humanity's survival.

conversation.text: Existential risk refers to threats that could cause human extinction or permanently curtail humanity's future.
Some researchers argue advanced AI poses an existential risk; others think the concern distracts from present harms.
Pandemics, nuclear war, and asteroid impacts are also studied as sources of existential risk.

senses.definition: Freed from any question of guilt, acquitted.
senses.example: Once fully exonerated, he returned to teaching at the same high school.

core.definition: Officially cleared of blame or guilt for a crime or wrongdoing, usually because new evidence shows innocence.
