The Greek word in Matthew 19:5 is proskollaō, meaning to cling to or cleave. 1 Timothy 3:2 (RSV) requires an overseer to be the husband of one wife, a phrase in the Greek (mias gynaikos andra) that Christian interpreters debate, some taking it as a rule about marital fidelity and others about remarriage.

senses.definition: During which no phase of the Moon is visible to provide light, whether because of cloud cover or because of a new moon.
senses.example: We drove into the desert on a moonless night and saw more stars than I'd ever seen.

senses.definition: Having no natural satellite.
senses.example: Mercury and Venus are both moonless, which surprised my students during the astronomy unit.

core.definition: Having no moon visible in the sky, usually because it is a new moon or because clouds hide it, so the night is very dark.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MOON-. The final syllable -less is a weak, reduced vowel, so say 'luhs', not 'less' with a strong e.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly ominous. It describes darkness, so it can suggest danger, mystery, or peace depending on the context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use moonless mainly for nights, skies, or places, such as 'a moonless night in the desert,' often when talking about camping, stargazing, or navigation. It is most common in descriptive writing and in weather or outdoor conversation. For a dark night in general, Americans may simply say 'pitch-black' or 'really dark.'

distinctions.note: Dark describes any lack of light, while moonless specifically means there is no moon in the sky.
New moon is the lunar phase when the Moon is not visible from Earth; moonless describes a sky or night without moonlight for any reason.

examples.everyday: We set up the tent under a moonless sky, so the stars were incredibly bright.
examples.professional: The night-vision test was scheduled on a moonless night to make the camera's low-light performance clear.
examples.analytical: In Milton's Paradise Lost, the moonless night serves as an image of the fallen world, where human reason cannot see clearly.

nuance.analogy: A moonless night is like a dark room with the lamp switched off, where only the stars give any light.
nuance.etymology: From moon (Old English mōna) plus the suffix -less, meaning 'without'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'moon-LESS'; the stress is on MOON.
Confusing it with 'moonlit', which means lit by the moon; the two words are opposites.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to the Moors or their culture.
Of or pertaining to a style of Spanish and Portuguese architecture from the time of the Moors, characterized by the horseshoe arch and ornate, geometric decoration.
senses.example: The palace courtyard features Moorish arches and intricate tilework from the fourteenth century.

core.definition: Relating to the Moors, the Muslim peoples of North Africa and medieval Spain, or to the art and architecture of their culture.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MOOR-, with an r-colored vowel. The ending -ish is a short 'ish', not 'eesh'; do not confuse it with 'more-ish'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and historical in architecture and art history, but it can carry sensitivity when used about people, so describe the culture carefully.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Moorish mainly in art history, architecture, and history courses, such as 'Moorish arches' or 'Moorish Revival' buildings in the US. In everyday conversation people usually say 'Spanish-style' or 'Islamic-style' decoration. Describe the people with care: Moorish refers to a historical group, not to all Arabs or to all Muslims.

distinctions.note: Arab refers to a broad ethnic and linguistic group, while Moorish refers specifically to the historical Muslim peoples of North Africa and Iberia.
Islamic refers to the religion and its traditions, while Moorish refers to a historical group and to styles of art and architecture linked to them.

examples.everyday: The café downtown has Moorish lanterns and tiled walls, which makes it feel like a different place.
examples.professional: The client wants a Moorish courtyard theme, so the vendor will need geometric tile and horseshoe arches.
examples.analytical: The Alhambra is often called the finest surviving Moorish palace, though its geometric and calligraphic design is best understood through Nasrid art history.

nuance.analogy: Moorish design is like a lace pattern carved in stone, with repeating geometry that fills a wall without a single figure.
nuance.etymology: From Moor, from Old French More, from Latin Maurus, possibly from Greek Mauros 'dark'.
common_mistakes: Using Moorish to mean all Arabs or all Muslims; it refers to a specific historical group.
Pronouncing it as 'more-ish', which is a British word meaning appetizing.

senses.definition: Capable of being moved, lifted, carried, drawn, turned, or conveyed, or in any way made to change place or posture; not fixed or stationary.
senses.example: The museum's movable exhibits let visitors rearrange the gallery each season.

senses.definition: Changing from one time to another.
senses.example: Easter is a movable holiday.

senses.definition: Something which is movable; an article of wares or goods; a commodity; a piece of property not fixed, or not a part of real estate; generally, in the plural, goods; wares; furniture.
senses.example: The estate sale included movables such as chairs, rugs, and an old piano.

core.definition: Able to be moved from one place to another; not fixed or permanently attached in one spot.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The -able ending is a weak, reduced 'uh-bul,' not 'ay-bull,' and the spelling 'moveable' is less common in American English.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a plain, practical description of objects or parts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans prefer the spelling 'movable' over 'moveable,' though both appear in dictionaries. 'Movable feast' is a special phrase for a holiday whose date changes from year to year, such as Easter. In everyday talk, 'movable' describes furniture, walls, or shelves that can be shifted.

distinctions.note: Portable means designed to be carried easily, while movable simply means able to be shifted from one place to another.
Mobile means able to move by itself or to be easily moved around, while movable means it can be moved by someone else.

examples.everyday: The kids' bed is movable, so we can shift it around when we repaint the room.
examples.professional: Please make the desks movable so the team can reconfigure the room for each workshop.
examples.analytical: A movable feast like Easter shows how a calendar can be governed by lunar and solar rules rather than fixed dates.

nuance.analogy: It is like a chess piece rather than a statue: it can be picked up and placed somewhere else.
nuance.etymology: From move plus -able; from Old French mouvable.
common_mistakes: Using 'moveable' as the normal American spelling, when 'movable' is more standard.
Confusing 'movable' (moved by someone else) with 'mobile' (able to move on its own).

senses.definition: A recorded sequence of images displayed on a screen at a rate sufficiently fast to create the appearance of motion; a film; a video.
senses.example: We watched a movie on Friday night, the first one we had seen together in years.

senses.definition: A professionally made motion picture of a substantive narrative work, typically around 1 to 3 hours long, typically intended for cinema, art, entertainment, and a widespread audience; a feature film, theatrical film.
senses.example: My favorite actor is starring in the new movie.

senses.definition: A cinema; a movie theater.
senses.example: Let's go to the movies.

senses.definition: Any event, especially one that is unpleasant or tiresome.
senses.example: Don't worry; this isn't the first time I've been through this movie.

senses.definition: An extremely fun and exciting experience.
senses.example: Every night with you is a movie!

core.definition: A film, a story shown in moving images on a screen, usually watched in a theater or at home.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final 'ie' is a plain 'ee' sound, not 'eye'. Keep the 'v' clear and do not turn it into a 'b'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is the ordinary everyday word, and 'film' sounds more critical or artistic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'movie' for almost any film, and 'go to the movies' means going to a cinema. 'Film' is more common in critical, academic, or industry settings, and 'motion picture' is formal. A typical reply to 'What do you want to do tonight?' is 'Let's see a movie.'

distinctions.note: 'Film' is more formal or artistic and common in criticism, while 'movie' is the everyday word.
'Motion picture' is formal and used in legal, industry or award contexts, rarely in casual talk.

examples.everyday: Want to watch a movie tonight? We can order food and stay in.
examples.professional: Our marketing team is promoting the movie's release in June.
examples.analytical: A movie's narrative structure can reveal how a culture understands memory, guilt and redemption.

nuance.analogy: Like a flipbook made of light, a movie tricks the eye into seeing motion.
nuance.etymology: 'Movie' is a shortening of 'moving picture', from Old English-derived 'move' and Latin pictura, 'painting'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable as 'eye' instead of 'ee'.
Saying 'go to the movie' when you mean the cinema; the plural 'movies' is standard for going out.

conversation.text: Do you want to see a movie tonight?
That movie was so good; you have to see it.
What movie are we watching tonight, something funny?

senses.definition: Low, indistinct (of a sound); reminiscent of a murmur.

core.definition: Low and indistinct, like a soft, continuous murmur; producing a quiet, blurred sound that is hard to make out.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and both r sounds are rhotic in General American. The final -ous is an unstressed 'us', not 'oos'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to gently positive. It suggests a soothing, unobtrusive sound, such as running water or distant voices, and it is rarely used for harsh or loud noise.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly meet this word in poetry, fiction and nature writing, not in everyday speech. In conversation you would more naturally say 'a low hum' or 'a quiet murmur'. Use it when you want a literary, slightly musical description of a soft, blurred sound.

distinctions.note: Murmuring is the everyday adjective or participle for a sound that is softly spoken or flowing; murmurous is more poetic and describes the quality of the sound itself.
Sonorous means deep, full and resonant, so it describes loud or rich sound; murmurous describes sound that is soft and hard to pick out.

examples.professional: The murmurous applause in the auditorium faded before the speaker had finished her last point.
examples.analytical: The poet's murmurous lines suggest a voice heard half-consciously, just beneath the threshold of meaning.

nuance.analogy: Like a creek you hear from another room: you know it is there, but you cannot make out any single word.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English murmuren, from Latin murmur, an imitative word for a low, continuous sound.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (mur-MUR-ous); the stress belongs on the first syllable.
Using murmurous for a sound that is clearly loud, where 'murmuring' or 'low' is not the right image.
Pronouncing the middle syllables as separate words; the word has three clear syllables: MUR-mur-us.

senses.definition: A contractile form of tissue which animals use to effect movement.
senses.example: Muscle consists largely of actin and myosin filaments.

senses.definition: An organ composed of muscle tissue.
senses.example: The heart is a muscle that never stops working, even while we sleep.

senses.definition: A well-developed physique, in which the muscles are enlarged from exercise.
senses.example: After a year of weightlifting, he finally built the muscle he had wanted.

senses.definition: Strength, force.
Hired strongmen or bodyguards.
senses.example: The mob boss sent muscle to collect the debts from the shop owners.

senses.definition: To use force to make progress, especially physical force.
senses.example: He muscled his way through the crowd.

senses.definition: To move forcefully or with great strength.
senses.example: She muscled through the ruins.

core.definition: Tissue in the body that contracts to move a body part, such as the arm, leg or heart. Also, strength or power in general.

pronunciation.tip: The c is silent, so the word sounds like 'MUS-uhl', with the final l often syllabic and no extra vowel. Stress falls on the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in the anatomy sense and positive in the strength sense, where it suggests power, fitness or influence.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use muscle in everyday talk about exercise, injuries and fitness: 'I pulled a muscle in my back.' The verb sense 'to muscle in' is informal and often negative, meaning to force your way into a situation where you are not wanted. Use 'muscle' for the body part, 'muscular' for the adjective, and avoid 'muscles' as a synonym for strength in formal writing.

distinctions.note: A tendon connects muscle to bone and transmits force, while a muscle generates the force by contracting.
Brawn means physical strength and size; muscle can mean the tissue itself or, informally, power or influence.

examples.everyday: I pulled a muscle in my back lifting boxes, so I'm taking it easy this weekend.
examples.professional: The ergonomics team says the warehouse lifting routine strains the lower back muscles.
examples.analytical: Galen's account of how muscle contracts raised questions that shaped early physiology for centuries.

nuance.analogy: A muscle is like a rope team: each fiber pulls only when told to, and together they move the whole load.
nuance.etymology: From Latin musculus, 'little mouse', perhaps from the shape of some muscles as they flex under the skin.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the silent c, as in 'MUS-kul'.
Saying 'muscle up' or 'muscle in' without the right sense; 'muscle in' means to force your way into something.
Confusing the noun muscle with the adjective muscular when describing a person's build.

muscle.etymology: From Middle English *muscle*, *muscule*, *muskylle*, and in part from Middle French *muscle*, from Latin *mūsculus* (“a muscle”) because of the mouselike appearance of some muscles, from *mūs* (“mouse”).

senses.definition: An object in a program that serves as a lock, used to negotiate mutual exclusion among threads.
To apply a mutex to.

core.definition: A lock in a program that allows only one thread at a time to use a shared resource.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The e is a short eh sound, and the word is one blended unit, not two words spoken separately.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical.
nuance.usage_note: Developers in American software teams use mutex in code, design reviews and discussions of concurrency bugs such as deadlocks. It is a technical term, so avoid it in ordinary conversation unless the listener is technical. In most languages, a thread acquires the mutex before entering a critical section and releases it afterward.

distinctions.note: A semaphore is a counter that can allow several threads at once; a mutex usually allows only one owner at a time.
Lock is the general term; mutex names a specific kind of lock that enforces mutual exclusion.

examples.everyday: The game freezes sometimes, and my friend said it's probably a mutex problem.
examples.professional: Let's protect the cache with a mutex so only one worker updates it at a time.
examples.analytical: A mutex enforces mutual exclusion, but careless ordering of acquisitions can still produce deadlock.

nuance.analogy: Like a single key to a bathroom: only one person can hold it at a time, and others must wait.
nuance.etymology: Short for mutual exclusion, from Latin mutuus, reciprocal, and exclusio, a shutting out.
common_mistakes: Confusing mutex with semaphore
Saying the word as two syllables, mute-ex, with a long u

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to mythology.

core.definition: Of or relating to mythology or to traditional myths; a rare form meaning mythological.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on LAH, and in General American the vowel in the second syllable of logic is the open 'ah' sound of cot. The -ic ending is a short 'ik'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and scholarly; it describes a subject or structure without emotion.
nuance.usage_note: Mythologic is rare in American English, and Americans almost always say mythological. Use mythologic only if you want a compact technical term or are reading older scholarship. In conversation, 'mythological creatures' or 'mythological stories' is the natural form.

distinctions.note: Mythological is the standard form with this meaning; mythologic is rarer and more compact.
Mythical means existing only in myth; mythologic describes a relation to myth as a body of stories or a way of thinking.

examples.everyday: My kids love the mythologic stories about Zeus, so we read them at bedtime.
examples.professional: The conference paper uses a mythologic framework to explain how founders' stories shape company culture.
examples.analytical: Lévi-Strauss reads the mythologic structure of a tale as a set of binary oppositions that reveal a deeper cultural logic.

nuance.analogy: Like a map of a country drawn from legends rather than surveys.
nuance.etymology: From Greek mythologia, from mythos (story) and logos (word, study).
common_mistakes: Choosing mythologic over mythological in ordinary speech, which sounds unusual to Americans.
Stressing the final syllable instead of LAH.

core.definition: A small town in Galilee, in northern Israel, where Jesus grew up and where the Gospels place the annunciation to Mary.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on the first syllable, NAZ. The second syllable is a reduced 'uh', and the final -eth is pronounced 'ith' in American speech. Avoid stressing the last syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a place name, used with respect in religious and historical contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say Nazareth as a town name in Bible study, travel, and church conversation, such as 'we visited Nazareth on our trip to Israel.' In casual talk, people sometimes add 'in Galilee' for clarity. The name is also used in phrases like Jesus of Nazareth.

distinctions.note: Nazareth is the place; Nazarene is a person from Nazareth or a religious name for Jesus and his followers.
Galilee is the larger region, while Nazareth is a town within it.

examples.everyday: We drove up to Nazareth on our trip to Israel, and the old streets were full of tourists.
examples.professional: The curriculum includes a unit on Nazareth and Galilee, so students understand Jesus' home setting.
examples.analytical: Luke places the annunciation in Nazareth, a detail that shapes how interpreters read Mary's social and religious context.

nuance.analogy: Nazareth is like a small hometown that becomes famous: the town is modest, but the name carries the story of the person who grew up there.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable (naz-uh-REETH); the stress is on NAZ.
Confusing Nazareth, the town, with Nazarene, the title or the person from there.
nuance.biblical_note: Nazareth is a village in Galilee where Jesus grew up. Luke 1:26 says that the angel Gabriel was sent to a city of Galilee named Nazareth to a virgin named Mary. Luke 4:16 describes Jesus coming to Nazareth, where he had been brought up, and entering the synagogue on the Sabbath. Matthew 2:23 says that Joseph came and dwelt in a city called Nazareth after the family returned from Egypt.

senses.definition: (historical) The custodian of a waqf, or Islamic endowment.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) A native official in an Anglo-Indian court who served summonses, etc.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: The manager or trustee who looks after an Islamic waqf, a charitable endowment, including its property, income, and expenses.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the second vowel short. Speakers of different backgrounds vary, so some may say NAH-zeer, but the short form is the safer American form.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a specialized legal and historical term with no social charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use nazir outside Islamic law, Middle Eastern and South Asian studies, or Anglo-Indian history. You would meet it in academic books or legal discussions about endowments. In everyday English, people would say trustee, manager, or administrator, and ask for an explanation if the term appears.

distinctions.note: Mutawalli is the more general term for an administrator of a waqf in many Islamic legal traditions, while nazir is common in South Asian and Anglo-Indian usage.
A qadi is an Islamic judge who decides legal cases, while a nazir manages property and funds.

examples.everyday: My colleague's grandfather was the nazir of a family endowment that funded a school in Lahore.
examples.professional: The nazir oversees rent collection, repairs, and accounts for the mosque's endowed properties.
examples.analytical: Colonial courts used the nazir as a court officer, showing how Anglo-Indian administration adapted older Islamic roles to new legal systems.

nuance.analogy: A nazir is like the property manager of a trust fund set up for a school or mosque, responsible for the assets without owning them.
nuance.etymology: From Arabic nāẓir, 'overseer' or 'supervisor'.
common_mistakes: Assuming a nazir is a judge, when the role is closer to a trustee or administrator.
Confusing nazir with nazarene, which is a different word with a different origin and meaning.

senses.definition: Of or relating to necromancy: the resurrection of or communication with the dead, especially through the use of black magic.
Conjuration.
senses.example: In the novel, the villagers feared necromantic more than plague, believing it summoned spirits from the grave.

core.definition: Relating to necromancy, the practice of communicating with the dead to predict the future or gain power, usually through dark magic.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, NEK. The second syllable has a lighter secondary stress, and the ending is a short 'tik', not a long 'tick'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests forbidden, sinister arts that disturb the natural order.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use necromantic outside literature, scholarship, fantasy and horror writing. In conversation people would say dark magic or black magic instead. It appears in discussions of Shakespeare, medieval witchcraft or ancient religion, and it sounds bookish but is clear and not rude.

distinctions.note: Necrotic describes dead body tissue, as in a necrotic wound; necromantic describes magic that summons the dead.
Occult is the broad word for hidden or magical knowledge; necromantic is narrower and refers only to contacting the dead.

examples.everyday: That horror movie was too creepy for me, with all the necromantic chanting in the cellar.
examples.professional: The editor asked the author to reduce the necromantic imagery in the second act so the magic would feel more consistent with the rest of the plot.
examples.analytical: The prophet's condemnation targets necromantic practices not because the dead are unreal but because such rites displace trust in God.

nuance.analogy: A necromantic ritual is like trying to finish a conversation with someone whose phone has been disconnected for decades.
nuance.etymology: From necromancy plus the suffix -ic, from Greek nekros (dead) and manteia (divination).
common_mistakes: Using necromantic as a noun for a practitioner; the noun is necromancer, and necromancy names the practice.
Stressing the second syllable, saying NEK-roh-MAN-tik; keep the main stress on NEK.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to a style of architecture based on classical models, especially such a style of the 18th century.
Of or relating to various art styles, as in sculpture and ballet, inspired by older classical forms and conventions.
senses.example: The museum's neoclassical sculptures echo the proportions of ancient Greek statues.

senses.definition: Being a recent construction based on older, classical elements.
senses.example: The English word "psychopathy" is a neoclassical compound from Ancient Greek roots.

senses.definition: Of or relating to an approach that focuses on the determination of prices, outputs, and income distributions in markets through supply and demand.
senses.example: The neoclassical model predicts that wages and prices adjust to balance supply and demand.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of neoclassical economist.

core.definition: Of or relating to a style of art, architecture or literature that revives classical Greek and Roman forms, especially in the 18th century.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on KLASS. The first syllable, nee, is a clear long e, and the ending -ical reduces to ih-kuhl.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It usually praises order, balance and restraint in art and design.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use neoclassical in art history, music, architecture and economics, as in "neoclassical architecture" or "neoclassical economics." Many American courthouses and government buildings are neoclassical. In everyday speech, people may say classical-style, but a museum guide or architect will normally say neoclassical.

distinctions.note: Classical refers to original ancient Greek or Roman works, while neoclassical refers to later works that imitate those models.
Baroque is the earlier, more ornate and dramatic style; neoclassical is more restrained, symmetrical and ordered.

examples.everyday: The courthouse downtown has neoclassical columns, so it looks like an old Greek temple.
examples.professional: Our design team is pitching a neoclassical look for the lobby, with stone columns and symmetrical proportions.
examples.analytical: Neoclassical art privileged reason and order over emotion, which is why later critics set it against Romanticism.

nuance.analogy: A neoclassical building is like a modern house that borrows the proportions of an ancient temple, keeping its columns and symmetry.
nuance.etymology: From neo- (new) and classical, from Latin classicus (of the highest class).
common_mistakes: Using classical for later imitations; classical refers to the original ancient works, while neoclassical refers to later revivals.
Stressing the neo syllable; the main stress falls on KLASS, so say nee-oh-KLASS-ih-kuhl.

senses.definition: Petty.
senses.example: Her niggling complaints about the font size delayed the report by two days.

senses.definition: Irritating.
A small irritating sensation.
senses.example: A niggling in my lower back reminded me to stop lifting boxes.

core.definition: Small and irritating; a minor worry, doubt, or problem that keeps bothering you and is hard to dismiss.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the second syllable short and light, like the -ling in 'tingling.' Do not stress the second syllable or add a separate vowel between g and l.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative; it describes a small problem or doubt that nags at you.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use niggling in writing and conversation for a small doubt or minor issue that won't go away, as in 'a niggling feeling I forgot something.' Some listeners hear the sound of a racial slur, so in speech with people who may be sensitive, nagging or lingering is safer. The word is still common in careful American writing.

distinctions.note: Nagging suggests repeated pressure from a person or a feeling, while niggling describes a small doubt or problem that stays in the mind.
Petty describes something trivial or mean-spirited, while niggling describes a small thing that persistently bothers you.

examples.everyday: I've got a niggling feeling I left the stove on, so I'm going to check.
examples.professional: I still have a niggling concern about the pipeline's timing, so let's review it before release.
examples.analytical: A niggling doubt about the argument's premise lingers even after the proof appears complete.

nuance.analogy: A niggling doubt is like a pebble in your shoe: small, but you keep feeling it with every step.
nuance.etymology: From the verb niggle, meaning to fuss over small things; the origin of niggle is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (nig-LING) instead of the first.
Confusing niggling with niggard, which means stingy; niggling is about small worries or problems.

senses.definition: In AI: Natural language processing: the field of AI that enables computers to understand and generate human language.
Initialism of neuro-linguistic programming.
senses.example: The corporate trainer spent the afternoon teaching us NLP techniques for communicating with clients.

senses.definition: Initialism of natural language processing.
Initialism of nonlinear programming.
senses.example: Our optimization model used NLP to find the cheapest production schedule under nonlinear constraints.

senses.definition: Initialism of neuro-linguistic psychotherapy. (Can we verify this sense?)
senses.example: The therapist's brochure described NLP, or neuro-linguistic psychotherapy, as a way to reframe habits.

senses.definition: Initialism of no light perception.
senses.example: The chart noted NLP for the patient, meaning no light perception in either eye after the injury.

core.definition: In AI, natural language processing: the field that enables computers to understand and generate human language.

pronunciation.tip: Say the letters, N-L-P, with the strongest stress on the last letter, PEE. Do not blend the letters into one word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term used in AI and data science.
nuance.usage_note: In American tech and data science work, NLP almost always means natural language processing. Outside those fields, some people use it for neuro-linguistic programming, a self-help idea that most scientists consider pseudoscience. Clarify the meaning if the context is unclear.

distinctions.note: NLU (natural language understanding) is the part of NLP focused on understanding meaning. NLP is the broader field, including generation.
NLG (natural language generation) is the part that produces text. NLP covers both understanding and generating language.

examples.everyday: My sister works in NLP at a tech company, so she's always building chatbots.
examples.professional: Our NLP pipeline classifies support tickets before they reach the team.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that current NLP systems predict word patterns without grasping meaning in the human sense.

nuance.analogy: Like a translator who knows the grammar and the meaning, not just the words, NLP lets a computer read and write language.
nuance.etymology: Initialism of natural language processing.
common_mistakes: Saying it as one word, 'nelp', instead of the three letters.
Assuming NLP always means neuro-linguistic programming, when in AI it means natural language processing.

conversation.text: Our NLP team handles everything from search to document classification.
Papers on large language models now dominate most NLP conferences.
Careful: in self-help circles, NLP means neuro-linguistic programming, which is something else entirely.

senses.definition: Absolutely not; no way.
senses.example: Do I think she'll go out with him? Not a chance.

core.definition: Absolutely not; there is no possibility at all that something will happen or be agreed to.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'chance', and the 'a' reduces to a quick schwa, so it sounds like 'uh'. The t of 'not' flaps before the vowel of 'a', so the phrase runs together as 'na-duh-CHANSS'.

nuance.connotation: Emphatic and casual; it firmly rejects a request or possibility. It can sound dismissive if said bluntly, though friends often say it playfully.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in casual talk when they are certain something will not happen, as in 'Will you finish the report by Friday? Not a chance.' A natural reply is 'Fair enough' or a laugh. In serious or formal settings, say 'That's very unlikely' or 'I don't think that's possible' instead.

distinctions.note: Both are emphatic refusals, but no way often expresses disbelief or surprise, while not a chance firmly rejects the possibility.
Not likely is a mild, polite estimate; not a chance is stronger and more emphatic.

examples.everyday: You want me to drive to the mall again? Not a chance, I'm watching the game.
examples.professional: Could the vendor deliver the new servers by Monday? Not a chance, the shipping delay is three weeks.
examples.analytical: The claim that a single anomaly could overturn the whole theory has not a chance unless it is replicated and explained.

nuance.analogy: A locked door with no key: the outcome is settled before anyone tries the handle.
common_mistakes: Doubling the negation, as in 'not no chance', which is ungrammatical in standard American English.
Using it in formal writing, where it sounds too casual.
Blurring the 'a' so the phrase sounds like 'nachance' with no stress on chance.

senses.definition: Pertaining to the nucleus of an atom.
Involving energy released by nuclear reactions (fission, fusion, radioactive decay).
senses.example: a nuclear reactor

senses.definition: Relating to a weapon that derives its force from rapid release of energy through nuclear reactions.
senses.example: a nuclear explosion

senses.definition: Having nuclear weapons.
Involving an extreme course of action, or one with severe consequences.
senses.example: nuclear option, nuclear solution

senses.definition: Pertaining to a center around which something is developed or organized; central, pivotal.
senses.example: Nuclear Polynesian languages include Hawaiian and Samoan.

senses.definition: Relating to, being of, or comprising the nuclear family.
senses.example: Our nuclear family spent every holiday together at my grandparents' farm.

senses.definition: Pertaining to the nucleus of a cell.
senses.example: The biologist stained the sample to make the nuclear membrane easier to see under the microscope.

senses.definition: Nuclear power.
senses.example: The state is debating whether nuclear should remain part of its long-term energy plan.

senses.definition: Nuclear weapon.
senses.example: The treaty limits how many nuclear weapons each country can keep in active storage.

core.definition: Relating to the nucleus of an atom, or to energy released by atomic reactions, such as nuclear power or nuclear weapons.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the middle syllable 'klee', not 'kyuh-ler'. Many Americans say NOO-klee-er, and the NYOO- variant is also heard; the final r is clearly pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in science and energy contexts; strongly negative or alarming when it refers to weapons or disasters.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nuclear every day in news, energy policy and science classes. Saying nucular is widely heard but is considered nonstandard by most educated speakers. Americans also use nuke as an informal verb (to microwave food, or to attack with nuclear weapons), which you should recognize but use carefully.

distinctions.note: Atomic is older and common in mid-century and historical contexts; nuclear is the standard technical term today.
Nucleic describes nucleic acids such as DNA and RNA; nuclear refers to the atomic nucleus or nuclear energy.

examples.everyday: My grandfather worked at a nuclear power plant for thirty years.
examples.professional: The nuclear safety review has to be finished before the reactor upgrade can move forward.
examples.analytical: Historians debate whether nuclear deterrence actually prevented great-power wars or only postponed them.

nuance.analogy: Like the sun at the center of a solar system, the nucleus anchors everything else in the atom.
nuance.etymology: From Latin nucleus, 'kernel' or 'core', a diminutive of nux, 'nut'.
common_mistakes: Saying NOO-kyuh-ler with three syllables, which many Americans hear as nonstandard; say NOO-klee-er.
Confusing nuclear with nucleic; nucleic acid is correct, and nuclear acid is wrong.

nuclear.etymology: From Latin *nū̆cleus*, a contraction of the adjective *nuculeus*, masculine of feminine *nuculea* (“pertaining to a small nut”) from *nucula* + adjectival suffix *-eus, -ea, -eum*.

senses.definition: To obstruct, cover, or otherwise block (an opening, a portion of an image, etc.).
senses.example: Thick fog began to occlude the lighthouse beam, forcing the captain to slow the ferry.

senses.definition: To absorb, as a gas by a metal.
senses.example: Palladium can occlude large volumes of hydrogen, which is why it is used in some fuel cell research.

core.definition: To block or close off an opening, passage, or view so that something cannot pass through or be seen.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, -KLUDE, and the first syllable is a weak schwa. Learners often stress the first syllable or pronounce the final d with an extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use occlude mostly in medicine, optics, dentistry, and science writing, where precision matters. In everyday speech they say block, close off, or cover. Saying the arteries were occluded is natural in a medical setting, but saying the hallway was occluded would sound stiff.

distinctions.note: Block is the everyday word and works for almost any obstruction; occlude is narrower and more technical, usually for openings, vessels, or images.
Obstruct emphasizes getting in the way of movement or progress; occlude emphasizes closing or covering an opening.

examples.everyday: A tree branch fell and partially occluded the driveway, so we had to park on the street.
examples.professional: The imaging software can detect when a lens cap or dust particle occludes part of the camera's field of view.
examples.analytical: Plato's allegory of the cave suggests that the shadows on the wall occlude the true forms from the prisoners' view.

nuance.analogy: Like a curtain drawn across a window, it blocks what lies behind without destroying it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin occludere, 'to shut up, close up,' from ob- 'against' plus claudere 'to shut.'
common_mistakes: Using occlude for everyday blocking, such as a parked car blocking a road; block is more natural.
Stressing the first syllable as OK-loo-d; the stress is on the second syllable.

occlude.etymology: Borrowed from Latin *occlūdere*, from *ob* (“before”) and *claudere* (“to shut”).

senses.definition: One who makes an offer to another; someone who presents something to another for acceptance or rejection.
senses.example: A unilateral contract consists of a promise on the part of the offeror and performance of the requisite terms by the offeree.

core.definition: A person or party who makes an offer to another, such as a proposal, bid or contract, for the other to accept or reject.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, AW-fer-er. The second syllable is a weak 'fer', and the ending is the reduced American r-sound, not the 'or' of 'door'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: a legal and business term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Offeror is the standard term in US contract law and business writing, while offerer is rarely used. In everyday talk Americans say 'the person making the offer' or simply 'the seller' or 'the buyer.' Use offeror in contracts, negotiations, or formal correspondence, and pair it with offeree, the party receiving the offer.

distinctions.note: Both mean one who offers, but offeror is the preferred legal and business term, while offerer is a rare, general word.
An offeror makes the offer and an offeree receives it; the two roles are opposite sides of the same deal.
A bidder names a price at an auction or tender, while an offeror makes an offer in ordinary negotiation or contract formation.

collocations: a binding offer from the offeror

examples.everyday: My cousin, who's a lawyer, says the seller is the offeror, so the offer can be pulled until I accept.
examples.professional: The offeror has until Friday to accept or withdraw, according to the term sheet we sent.
examples.analytical: Under contract doctrine, the offeror keeps control of the terms until the offeree accepts, which is why an offer can usually be revoked before acceptance.

nuance.analogy: Think of the offeror as the person holding the door open; the other party decides whether to walk through.
nuance.etymology: From offer plus the Latin agent suffix -or, meaning one who does the action.
common_mistakes: Using offeror in casual speech, where 'the person offering' sounds more natural.
Confusing offeror with offeree, the party who receives the offer.

senses.definition: Frequently; many times on different occasions.
senses.example: I often walk to work when the weather is nice.

core.definition: Frequently; on many occasions or at short intervals.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The t is usually silent in General American, so it sounds like 'OFF-en,' but many speakers pronounce the t, so 'OFF-ten' is also common.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes frequency without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use often in every kind of speech and writing, as in 'I often go running.' Its position matters: before a main verb ('I often walk'), after 'be' ('I am often late'), and at the end for emphasis ('I go there, often'). Phrases like 'more often than not' and 'every so often' are very common in casual speech.

distinctions.note: Frequently is a bit more formal and precise, often used in writing or reports, while often is the everyday choice.
Usually means in most cases or as a normal pattern, while often means many times, not necessarily most of the time.

examples.everyday: We often grab tacos on Fridays after the kids' soccer practice.
examples.professional: We often find that the bug only appears under heavy load, so we should test with production-sized data.
examples.analytical: Philosophers have often noted that intuitions about moral cases shift with the way the case is framed.

nuance.analogy: Often is like rain in Seattle: it shows up a lot, but not every single day.
nuance.etymology: From Old English oft 'frequently'; the -en spelling was added in Middle English.
common_mistakes: Placing it wrongly, as in 'I go often to the gym' instead of 'I often go to the gym.'
Using often as an adjective in everyday speech; use frequent instead.

often.etymology: From Middle English *often*, alteration of Middle English *ofte*, *oft*, from Old English *oft* (“often”), from Proto-Germanic **ufta*, **uftō* (“often”).

senses.definition: In a state of elation; very happy; blissful.
senses.example: When her offer letter arrived, she was on cloud nine all afternoon.

core.definition: Extremely happy and excited, feeling wonderful about something good that has happened.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on NINE, with a lighter stress on CLOUD. 'On' reduces to 'un' in fast speech, and the 'ou' in 'cloud' is a diphthong that moves from 'ah' to 'oo'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it celebrates happiness, often after good news such as a job offer, engagement, or a win.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say on cloud nine in casual speech about personal happiness, such as a new baby or a promotion. It is usually used for a person, as in 'She's on cloud nine since the wedding.' A natural reply is 'That's wonderful! Congratulations!'. It sounds a bit playful, so avoid it in very formal writing.

distinctions.note: Happy is a general word; on cloud nine suggests a much stronger, almost euphoric joy that is temporary.
Over the moon is a similar idiom with the same strong joy, but it is slightly more common in British speech; Americans use both.

collocations: on cloud nine since the wedding
on cloud nine about the news

examples.everyday: My sister got the job she wanted, and she's been on cloud nine all week.
examples.professional: After the funding round closed, the whole team was on cloud nine, but we still had a long roadmap to finish.
examples.analytical: Philosophers of happiness distinguish moments of elation, which are like being on cloud nine, from lasting well-being that is more modest and stable.

nuance.analogy: Being on cloud nine is like floating above everyday worries, light enough to drift without any weight.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain; often linked to the highest category in an early meteorological classification of clouds.
common_mistakes: Saying 'on the cloud nine' with an article; the phrase is 'on cloud nine'.
Pronouncing 'nine' as 'nein' or with a short vowel; it rhymes with 'wine'.

conversation.text: She's been on cloud nine since she got engaged.
We were on cloud nine after closing the biggest deal of the year.
When the baby was born, I was on cloud nine.
They're on cloud nine with the new baby.

senses.definition: By design, as opposed to by accident; intentionally; deliberately.
senses.example: That wasn't an accident! You did it on purpose!

senses.definition: In order to (do something); with the objective that.
senses.example: They moved closer to the city on purpose, in order to shorten their commutes.

core.definition: Intentionally, by plan or choice, rather than by accident.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PUR, the first syllable. The second syllable is weak, like 'pus', and the r is pronounced, so the vowel is r-colored, not 'pope'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in simple contexts, but it implies blame when describing something bad, such as 'You did that on purpose.'
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'on purpose' constantly in everyday speech, both to deny and to accuse. Saying 'I didn't do it on purpose' is a common apology. A natural reply is 'I know, it's okay.' The second meaning, 'in order to,' is rarer and more formal.

distinctions.note: Purposely is a close synonym that emphasizes the deliberate planning behind an action.
Intentionally is more formal and common in legal and academic writing.
Deliberately is formal and suggests careful thought and consideration, often for a negative action.

examples.everyday: I didn't break your mug on purpose, I swear. It slipped out of my hand.
examples.professional: We left the old endpoint running on purpose so partners can migrate on their own schedule.
examples.analytical: Whether a harm was done on purpose or through negligence changes how we assign moral responsibility.

nuance.analogy: Like an archer aiming at a target rather than letting an arrow fly loose.
nuance.etymology: From Old French purpos, from purposer, 'to propose'; the phrase means with a plan in mind.
common_mistakes: Writing 'by purpose' instead of 'on purpose'.
Saying 'on the purpose' instead of 'on purpose'.

senses.definition: Atop.
senses.example: There's a house on top of the mountain.

senses.definition: Very close to, in any orientation or in time.
senses.example: Living on top of one another in a refugee camp is stressful.

senses.definition: In addition to something else.
senses.example: […] and on top of all that, I got a puncture!

senses.definition: Fully informed about, and in control of, something; up to speed with.
senses.example: I have sorted out the problems and am now on top of the situation.

core.definition: Directly on or above something; also meaning in addition to something, often a problem or burden.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on top, and of is reduced to uhv. The f in of is pronounced as a v in this weak position, so the phrase flows as ahn-TAHP-uhv.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when physical; negative when it means an extra burden, as in 'on top of everything else,' which expresses frustration. Positive when it means staying informed.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it for physical position, as in 'The cat jumped on top of the fridge,' and very often to stack problems, as in 'On top of work, I have to move this weekend.' With a negative tone it signals being overwhelmed. It can also be positive, as in 'She's really on top of her emails,' meaning she handles them well.

distinctions.note: On top of that is a complete phrase used to add a point; on top of is a preposition that needs an object.
In addition to is more formal and neutral; on top of often signals an extra burden or problem.

examples.everyday: The cat jumped on top of the fridge again, and now I can't get her down.
examples.professional: On top of the migration work, we also have to handle three new compliance requests this sprint.
examples.analytical: On top of the methodological problems, the study ignores selection bias, which makes its causal claims hard to accept.

nuance.analogy: Like a stack of plates: each new one goes right on top of the last.
common_mistakes: Dropping of and saying on top the table
Using it with a time sense, when right after is clearer

core.definition: A town in the territory of Benjamin, mentioned in Scripture as a place rebuilt after the exile and near the valley of Ono.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, OH. Pronounce the final vowel as a clear oh sound, not a reduced uh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a proper place name with no everyday meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Ono almost only in Bible study, archaeology, or discussion of the Old Testament. It is not a common everyday word. In a Bible study, you would say that Ono was a town in Benjamin rebuilt after the exile.

distinctions.note: Lod is a neighboring town that is often mentioned together with Ono in Ezra and Nehemiah, so the two are commonly paired.

examples.everyday: Our Bible study group read about the town of Ono in Nehemiah this week.
examples.professional: In the seminar lecture, the professor placed Ono in the Shephelah region near Lod.
examples.analytical: The reference to the plain of Ono in Nehemiah 6:2 shows that the place was known as a settled area in the postexilic period.

nuance.analogy: Ono is like a small hometown that appears on a few lists of places in a family's history, important only to those tracing that story.
nuance.etymology: From the Hebrew place name Ono; the meaning is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Saying it as AW-no, which is not the standard pronunciation.
Confusing Ono with the Japanese word for a different meaning, which is unrelated.
nuance.biblical_note: Ono (Hebrew Ono) is a town in the territory of Benjamin, listed among places resettled by the returned exiles. In 1 Chronicles 8:12 Ono is linked with the founding of Lod. In Ezra 2:33 its men are counted among those who returned. In Nehemiah 6:2 Sanballat proposes a meeting in one of the villages of the plain of Ono, which Nehemiah refuses.

senses.definition: The act or process of operationalizing.

core.definition: The process of turning an abstract idea into specific, measurable steps or indicators so it can be studied or tested.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on -ZAY- near the end, and the -al- is weak, so it sounds like 'luh' rather than 'al'. Many learners put the stress on -RAY- instead.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a precise research term that can sound jargon-heavy or pedantic outside academic settings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this mainly in social science, psychology, statistics, and data science when discussing how to measure a concept. In everyday talk, people say 'how we'll measure it' or 'how we define it'. It works best in academic writing, research design discussions, and careful debates.

distinctions.note: A conceptual definition explains what a term means; operationalization specifies how you will measure it.
Measurement is the act of collecting data; operationalization is the design step that decides what to measure and how.

examples.everyday: You can't really argue about whether a city is walkable until someone does the operationalization of what walkable means.
examples.professional: Our survey's operationalization of customer satisfaction was too vague, so we're rewriting the questions before launch.
examples.analytical: The operationalization of intelligence as a single test score is a choice that shapes what the research can ever conclude about it.

nuance.analogy: Like turning a recipe's 'tasty' into exact measurements: two tablespoons of salt, eight minutes at 375 degrees.
nuance.etymology: From Latin operari 'to work'; the idea was popularized by physicist Percy Bridgman in 1927.
common_mistakes: Putting the main stress on -RAY- as in 'operation'; the main stress falls on -ZAY- near the end.

senses.definition: A person trained and skilled in examining and testing the eyes for defects, in order to prescribe corrective lenses or treatment.
senses.example: My optometrist found a slight astigmatism and prescribed new glasses for reading and driving.

core.definition: A health professional who examines eyes, checks vision, and prescribes glasses or contact lenses.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'TAH' in the second syllable. The 'r' is pronounced clearly before 'ist' in American speech, and the first vowel is 'ah' rather than 'op.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and professional. It names a licensed eye-care provider.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'optometrist' when talking about routine eye exams and glasses, and 'ophthalmologist' for an eye doctor who is a medical physician and handles surgery or disease. An optometrist usually cannot perform eye surgery. Saying 'I'm seeing my optometrist next week' is natural in casual talk.

distinctions.note: An ophthalmologist is a medical doctor who can perform eye surgery and treat serious eye disease; an optometrist examines vision and prescribes lenses.
An optician fits and sells glasses and contacts based on a prescription; an optometrist writes the prescription after examining the eyes.

examples.everyday: I need to make an appointment with my optometrist, because my glasses are giving me headaches.
examples.professional: The clinic's optometrist reviewed the vision screening results and referred two patients to ophthalmology.
examples.analytical: The distinction between optometrist and ophthalmologist reflects a division of labor in which the first measures refraction and the second treats disease.

nuance.analogy: Like a mechanic who checks the alignment and tunes the lenses of your eyes, rather than performing major surgery.
nuance.etymology: From Greek optos, 'seen,' with -metry (measurement) and -ist (practitioner).
common_mistakes: Confusing 'optometrist' with 'ophthalmologist' and assuming the optometrist can do surgery.
Stressing the first syllable as 'OP-tom-e-trist' instead of 'ahp-TAH-muh-trist.'

conversation.text: I go to the optometrist once a year for an eye exam.
The optometrist said my vision has changed a little.
Is there an optometrist inside the mall?

senses.definition: The concept that everything is organic, or forms part of an organic whole.
senses.example: Her dissertation traced organicism through nineteenth-century social thought, from Herder to Spencer.

senses.definition: The treatment of society or the universe as if it were an organism.
The mereological idea that living things are the only composite objects.
senses.example: In his metaphysics seminar, the professor defended organicism, holding that only living things form genuine composite objects.

senses.definition: The theory that the total organization of an organism is more important than the functioning of its individual organs.
senses.example: The physiologist's organicism rejected reductionism, insisting that the whole organism mattered more than any single organ.

senses.definition: (historical) The theory that disease is a result of structural alteration of organs.
senses.example: Nineteenth-century physicians who embraced organicism blamed illness on lesions in the tissues of particular organs.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: The philosophical view that society, nature, or the universe should be understood as a living whole whose parts depend on one another, not as separate pieces.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on GAN, and the 'ic' in the middle is pronounced like the 's' in 'criticism', so it is 'siz-um' rather than 'kiz-um'. The final syllable is a reduced 'um', not a full 'ism'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a descriptive term in philosophy and intellectual history, not a value judgment, though critics may use it to suggest that a view is vague or overly holistic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly meet this word in philosophy, political theory, and the history of ideas, such as discussions of Romantic thinkers. It is not everyday vocabulary and would sound pretentious in casual talk. Do not confuse it with 'organic' food labels; in the US, organic means grown without synthetic pesticides, which has nothing to do with this philosophy.

distinctions.note: Holism is the broad idea that wholes are more than the sum of their parts; organicism is a specific holism that models the whole on a living organism.
Mechanism treats the world as a machine built from separate parts, the opposite stance to organicism's view of an integrated living whole.

examples.everyday: My uncle has this organicism idea that everything in nature is connected, so he talks about it every time we go hiking.
examples.professional: The architect's proposal relies on a kind of organicism, treating the whole campus as one living system instead of a set of separate buildings.
examples.analytical: Coleridge's political writing draws on organicism, describing the state as a living whole in which each part gets its meaning from the body politic.

nuance.analogy: Like a tree, where every root, branch, and leaf makes sense only as part of one living plant.
nuance.etymology: From 'organic' plus '-ism'; 'organic' comes from Greek organikos, relating to an organon, an instrument or tool.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'organic' in the sense of food or chemicals, which changes the meaning completely.
Putting the stress on the final syllable instead of GAN.

senses.definition: Apparently true, but not necessarily; ostensible.
senses.example: The ostensive reason for the delay was a broken valve, though the real cause remained unclear.

senses.definition: Clearly demonstrative.

core.definition: Showing or demonstrating something directly, as by pointing; also, apparent or stated on the surface, which may not be the real reason or fact.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, -TEN-, and the ending -sive is short and unstressed, like 'siv' rather than 'seev'. Learners often confuse it with 'ostensible' (/ɑˈstɛnsəbəl/), which has the same root but a different ending and stress pattern.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In philosophy and linguistics it is a technical description, but in general speech it can imply that something is being staged or that the stated reason hides a different one.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English people say 'ostensible' for the sense 'apparent but possibly false', and 'ostensibly' is very common, as in 'ostensibly for work'. Ostensive is mainly used in philosophy, linguistics and formal writing, especially in the phrase 'ostensive definition', which means explaining a word by pointing to examples. Using it in casual conversation will sound stiff, so say 'supposed' or 'official' instead.

distinctions.note: Ostensible means apparent or claimed, and is the common word for 'on the surface', while ostensive is mainly about showing or pointing directly.
Explicit means stated clearly and directly in words, whereas ostensive refers to showing something by demonstration or gesture.

examples.everyday: He gave an ostensive reason for leaving early, but I think he was just tired of the party.
examples.professional: The ostensive purpose of the meeting was to review the roadmap, but leadership really wanted to talk about the budget.
examples.analytical: Wittgenstein's critique of ostensive definition shows that pointing at an object cannot fix the meaning of a word without a shared understanding of how the word is used.

nuance.analogy: A parent pointing at a dog and saying 'dog' is giving an ostensive definition, showing the meaning instead of describing it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin ostendere, 'to show, display', via the Late Latin ostensivus.
common_mistakes: Using ostensive where ostensible is meant, as in 'his ostensive reason'; say 'ostensible reason' instead.
Stressing the first syllable, as in 'OS-ten-sive', instead of the second, 'os-TEN-sive'.

ostensive.etymology: From Middle French *ostensif* and its etymon Late Latin *ostēnsīvus*.

senses.definition: To judge or calculate too highly.
senses.example: I overestimated the number of attendees, and bought far too much food for the party.

senses.definition: An estimate that is too high.
senses.example: Our first budget was an overestimate, and we ended up with extra money.

core.definition: To judge or calculate something as larger, better or more important than it really is.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on ES, the second syllable, and the ending -mate sounds like mayt. Keep the middle syllable a quick r-colored schwa rather than oh-vuh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative: it implies an error in judgment, but it is polite when you admit your own misjudgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use overestimate in planning, budgets and everyday talk, as in 'I overestimated how long the drive would take.' It describes an honest mistake, so it sounds softer than saying someone is wrong. A natural reply is 'Yeah, we both did, it took three hours.'

distinctions.note: Exaggerate implies deliberately making something sound bigger, while overestimate usually means a sincere error in judgment.
Overrate means valuing someone or something too highly in quality or reputation, not in amounts or time.

examples.everyday: I think I overestimated how much pizza we needed for the party.
examples.professional: We overestimated demand for the new feature, so the servers sat mostly idle all week.
examples.analytical: Early studies overestimated the effect size, and later replications could not reproduce it.

nuance.analogy: Overestimating is like a bathroom scale set five pounds too heavy: you believe the number is higher than the truth.
nuance.etymology: From over- (too much) and estimate, from Latin aestimare, to value.
common_mistakes: Using overestimate for deliberate exaggeration; that is closer to exaggerate.
Confusing overestimate with overrate when you mean a movie or book is too highly praised.

senses.definition: Pertaining to the textual relationality of a palimpsest; referential to earlier works or self-referential between several meanings of a single text.

core.definition: Describing a text that refers back to earlier works or holds several meanings at once, the way a palimpsest keeps earlier writing visible.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on SES, with the ending pronounced 'choo-us', like the ch in 'virtuous.' Do not stress the final syllable or say the ending as 'uss'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and specialized. It is used in critical writing to praise or describe complex intertextual works.
nuance.usage_note: This is a rare, specialized coinage from literary theory, seen mostly in scholarship on intertextuality. Americans would seldom use it in conversation. For everyday talk, say that the book echoes or depends on earlier works.

distinctions.note: Palimpsestic is the common term for layered writing or physical erasure; palimpsestuous is narrower and stresses the relationship between texts.
Intertextual is the standard academic term for texts that refer to other texts; palimpsestuous adds the sense of earlier meaning showing through.
Allusive describes a text that hints at earlier works, while palimpsestuous emphasizes that the earlier layer remains partly visible.

examples.professional: The codebase is palimpsestuous: old comments and deprecated functions still show through the refactor, and everyone reads them differently.
examples.analytical: Borges's stories are palimpsestuous, because each apparent source text is also a commentary that changes the meaning of the others.

nuance.analogy: Like a song that quotes an older melody, so listeners hear the new tune and the old one underneath at the same time.
nuance.etymology: Formed from palimpsest with the adjective suffix -uous, on the model of words such as sensuous; the coinage is rare and literary-critical.
common_mistakes: Using palimpsestuous for any complicated text; it is a specialized critical term.
Pronouncing the ending as -uss; it is choo-us, with a ch sound.

palimpsestuous.etymology: From *palimpsest* + *-ous* by surface analysis, but also a humorous *palimpsest* + *incestuous*.

senses.definition: In a panoramic way.
senses.example: The software let users scroll panoramically across the entire timeline of sensor readings.

core.definition: In a way that shows a wide, sweeping view of a whole scene, all at once.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on RAM, the third syllable, with a light secondary stress on pan. Keep the short a in RAM and reduce the ending to -lee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes how something is displayed or observed.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use panoramically mostly in photography, software, real estate, and descriptive writing. In everyday speech they usually say 'in panoramic view' or use the adjective panoramic. The word describes how a scene is shown or seen, not how large it is. For example, a phone app can scan a room panoramically.

distinctions.note: Broadly means in general terms; panoramically means seeing or showing a wide view all at once.
Comprehensively stresses complete coverage of every detail; panoramically stresses breadth over depth.

examples.everyday: Hold your phone steady and the app will scan the whole room panoramically.
examples.professional: The dashboard shows regional sales panoramically, so the whole team can see the trend in one view.
examples.analytical: The historian surveys the period panoramically, though this breadth sacrifices depth in individual cases.

nuance.analogy: Like standing on a ridge: you see the whole valley at once, not one tree at a time.
nuance.etymology: From panoramic, from Greek pan 'all' and horama 'view'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable or using a long a in RAM, as in 'pan-uh-RAY-mik'.
Using panoramically to mean in detail or thoroughly; it means broadly, not in depth.

senses.definition: Complete and universal knowledge, or a system of such universal knowledge.

core.definition: Complete and universal knowledge, or a system that claims to contain all human knowledge in a unified form.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, PAN. The second syllable is a reduced schwa, and the final -y sounds like 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative, since it can suggest an overambitious claim to know everything.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use pansophy today, except in discussions of intellectual history, such as the seventeenth-century educational reformer Comenius. Outside that context, people say encyclopedic knowledge or a broad education. Using it in ordinary talk may sound pretentious.

distinctions.note: Omniscience is the state of knowing everything, often attributed to God; pansophy is a body or system of universal knowledge.
An encyclopedia is a reference work organized alphabetically; pansophy refers to a philosophical ideal or system aiming at a unified picture of all knowledge.

examples.everyday: Old books promised a kind of pansophy, but my grandmother just said nobody can know everything.
examples.professional: Their pitch deck promised a pansophy of marketing data, which sounded impressive but gave us nothing we could act on.
examples.analytical: Comenius's Pansophia sought a unified system of all human knowledge, a project that presupposed the unity of truth.

nuance.analogy: Pansophy is like a single map that claims to show every road, river and mountain in the world at once.
nuance.etymology: From Greek pan, 'all', and sophia, 'wisdom'.
common_mistakes: Using pansophy for ordinary knowledge; it means a claim to universal knowledge.
Stressing the second syllable, which is weak.

pansophy.etymology: Originally from Ancient Greek *pan-* + *-sophy*, then from Latin *pansophia* to English.

senses.definition: Dad, daddy, father; a familiar or old-fashioned term of address to one’s father.
A pet name for one's grandfather.
A parish priest in the Greek Orthodox Church.
senses.example: Father Nikolaos, the local papa, blessed the new bakery after the Easter liturgy.

core.definition: Dad or daddy, a familiar or old-fashioned name for one's father, sometimes used affectionately for a grandfather.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, with an open ah sound like the vowel in father. Keep the second syllable short and reduced, not PAH-PAH and not the French-style pah-PAH.

nuance.connotation: Affectionate and warm, but sometimes old-fashioned or sentimental. It suits family speech and storytelling more than casual adult chat.
nuance.usage_note: Americans more often say Dad, Daddy, or Pop, and papa sounds affectionate or old-fashioned. Some families use it for a grandfather, and it appears in older books and songs. In Greek Orthodox churches, papas can be a priest, a sense you may hear at a church event.

distinctions.note: Dad is the everyday American word for father, while papa is warmer, more old-fashioned, or used within a particular family.
Pop is a casual American term, often used by adult children, while papa is more tender or formal-sounding.

examples.everyday: Papa, can you pick me up from soccer at five o'clock?
examples.professional: My supervisor always talks about her papa, who taught her to balance a checkbook before she ever learned to write code.
examples.analytical: In Freud's account, the figure of the papa carries an authority that the child both fears and imitates.

nuance.analogy: Papa is like a warm family nickname that stays fixed on the family photo album, even as everyone else moves on to Dad.
nuance.etymology: From Greek pappas and Latin papa, father, a word widely used by young children across languages.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, like the Spanish pah-PAH, instead of PAH-puh.
Confusing papa with pope, which is the title of the bishop of Rome and comes from the same root.

papa.etymology: From French *papa*, from Middle French *papa*, from Old French *papa*, from Latin *papa*, probably originally a reduplicated of a child's early efforts at vocalising Latin *pater* (“father”).

senses.definition: Routine work involving written documents.
senses.example: do paperwork

senses.definition: Written documents.
Excessive paperwork, busy work, red tape.
senses.example: Filing the insurance claim meant hours of paperwork and endless phone calls.

senses.definition: Court documents or pre-sentencing investigation reports detailing the prisoner's criminal history (usually in the context of discerning whether an inmate has been charged for sex-related offenses or is likely to be an informant).
senses.example: to have bad paperwork

senses.definition: A work in paper.

core.definition: Routine work involving forms, records, and written documents, or the documents themselves.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PAY, and wurk has a secondary stress. The middle -er is reduced, and the r in work is strongly pronounced in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral, often suggesting tedium or bureaucracy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use paperwork constantly at work, at the doctor's office, and when buying a house or car, often with a complaining tone. It is uncountable, so say 'a lot of paperwork' rather than 'a lot of paperworks.' A common reply is 'Tell me about it, the forms never end.'

distinctions.note: Documents are the individual written items, while paperwork refers to the overall administrative tasks or the collection of forms.
Red tape describes excessive rules that slow processes, while paperwork is the neutral term for documents and forms.

examples.everyday: Buying the house involved so much paperwork that I still have folders in my car.
examples.professional: Most of my week goes to paperwork: expense reports, approval forms, and status updates.
examples.analytical: Bureaucratic paperwork can obscure the moral choices behind administrative decisions, because each form makes responsibility seem diffuse.

nuance.analogy: Like a river of forms that keeps rising the faster you swim.
nuance.etymology: Compound of paper and work, the sense of documents and routine record-keeping.
common_mistakes: Using 'paperworks' as a plural; the word is uncountable.
Saying 'a paperwork' instead of 'a piece of paperwork' or 'a form'.

senses.definition: The conic section formed by the intersection of a cone with a plane parallel to a tangent plane to the cone; the locus of points equidistant from a fixed point (the focus) and line (the directrix).
senses.example: The satellite dish has a parabola shape that reflects incoming signals to a single point.

senses.definition: Synonym of parable.

core.definition: A symmetrical U-shaped curve, the graph of a quadratic function, defined by points equally distant from a focus and a directrix line.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, RAB. The first and last syllables are weak, so the word sounds like 'puh-RAB-uh-luh', with a clear American r.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It has no emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use parabola in math, physics and engineering classes, and when describing trajectories or satellite dishes. In a math class you will hear it used precisely, so use the technical sense. Do not confuse it with the everyday word parable, which is a story.

distinctions.note: Parable is a moral story; parabola is a geometric curve. They share a Greek root but mean entirely different things.
An ellipse is a closed oval curve, while a parabola is open and has only one branch.

examples.everyday: When you throw a ball, its path looks like a parabola.
examples.professional: The engineer modeled the water jet as a parabola to estimate how far it would reach.
examples.analytical: A parabola can be defined purely by a focus and a directrix, which shows how a curve can be fixed by a geometric relationship alone.

nuance.analogy: A parabola is the path a thrown basketball follows as it rises and falls in a smooth arc.
nuance.etymology: From Greek parabole, meaning application or comparison, used in geometry by Apollonius.
common_mistakes: Confusing parabola with parable, which is a story, not a shape.
Stressing the middle syllable of the wrong part of the word, as in 'PAR-uh-bola'.

parabola.etymology: Borrowed from New Latin *parabola*, from Ancient Greek *παραβολή*, from *παραβάλλω* (“to set side by side”), from *παρά* (“beside”) + *βάλλω* (“to throw”).

senses.definition: Synonym of parking space.
senses.example: I circled the garage twice before finding a parking spot near the office entrance.

core.definition: A marked place on a street or in a lot where one car can park.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SPOT, and the r in PAHR is strong. The final t is often a light stop or flap, and the vowel in spot is the same as in cot.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, friendly and everyday.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use parking spot in casual speech as a synonym of parking space, which is the more formal term on signs and in official texts. You can say I found a spot or I found a parking spot in conversation. People often say a spot to mean a place you can use. A natural reply is Nice, that is hard to find downtown.

distinctions.note: Parking space is the more formal or official term on signs and in laws, while parking spot is informal and everyday.
A parking spot is one place for one car, while a parking lot is the whole area with many spots.

examples.everyday: I finally found a parking spot near the coffee shop, so we can walk from here.
examples.professional: There are not enough parking spots for visitors, so we should book a shuttle for the conference.
examples.analytical: A parking spot is a scarce unit of urban space, and its allocation shows how cities balance mobility and access.

nuance.analogy: A parking spot is like a chair at a crowded table, one seat that only one person can use at a time.
common_mistakes: Using spot in a formal document where parking space is expected.
Saying parking spots with a stress on spots, which sounds unnatural.

conversation.text: I circled for twenty minutes looking for a parking spot.
Someone took my parking spot while I was backing in.
She found a parking spot right in front of the restaurant.

senses.definition: A check or direct deposit for wages or salary paid to an employee.
The amount of money a person is paid each pay period; one's regular income.

core.definition: The wages you receive from your employer each pay period, now usually by direct deposit rather than a paper check.

pronunciation.tip: Stress PAY, the first syllable; 'check' is lighter. It is one word, said quickly as a compound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; 'living paycheck to paycheck' suggests financial strain.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say paycheck even when the money arrives by direct deposit. Most are paid weekly, biweekly (every two weeks) or twice a month; the breakdown of taxes and deductions is on the pay stub. British English says 'pay packet' or 'payslip' for related ideas.

distinctions.note: Salary is your fixed annual pay; a paycheck is each individual payment of it.
A pay stub is the statement showing gross pay, taxes and deductions; the paycheck is the money itself.
Take-home pay is the amount left after deductions, which is what your paycheck actually delivers.

examples.everyday: I'll buy the new tires after my next paycheck comes in.
examples.professional: HR confirmed that the raise will show up on your first paycheck in March.
examples.analytical: Survey data suggest that many middle-income households, not only low-income ones, live paycheck to paycheck.

nuance.etymology: A compound of pay and check, the American spelling of cheque.
common_mistakes: Writing 'pay cheque' (British spelling) or 'pay check' as two words; Americans write paycheck.

conversation.text: I get paid every other Friday, so I'll pay you back after my next paycheck.
A lot of families here are living paycheck to paycheck.

senses.definition: Annoyed.

core.definition: Mildly annoyed or irritated, usually by someone's behavior or a small inconvenience.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a long ee and a final v followed by d. Don't add a syllable like 'PEE-ved'.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative; lighter than angry, and often used with a touch of humor.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'peeved' in casual talk for mild irritation, often about small things like a late delivery. You can say 'I'm kind of peeved' or 'She was peeved at him' to show a light complaint. It is less serious than 'livid' and sounds a bit old-fashioned in very formal settings.

distinctions.note: Annoyed is broader and more common; peeved suggests a slightly sulky or petty irritation.
Irate means angry, often strongly; peeved is much milder.
