pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, SPEN. The ending -ed is pronounced as a separate syllable, /ɪd/, so say suh-SPEN-did.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses; it can sound negative when it describes a punishment, such as a suspended license.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use suspended for games or meetings stopped because of weather or problems, for students suspended from school, and for a driver's license that has been taken away for a time. A suspended ceiling is a drop ceiling in an office. Suspended animation is a literary or medical phrase, and in everyday talk people say that something is on hold.

distinctions.note: Postponed means moved to a later date; suspended means stopped for now, with the possibility of resuming it.
Canceled means it will not happen at all, while suspended means it is paused and may continue later.
Expelled is a permanent removal, while suspended is a temporary removal from a school, team, or job.

examples.everyday: My driver's license got suspended after too many speeding tickets, so I'm taking the bus for a while.
examples.professional: The rollout is suspended until the security review is finished, so please don't push any changes.
examples.analytical: The argument remains suspended between two incompatible premises, and the author never resolves that tension.

nuance.analogy: A suspended process is like a ball held in midair: it is neither finished nor falling, and it can drop again.
nuance.etymology: From Latin suspendere 'to hang up', through the past participle suspensus, and the English past-participle form suspended.
common_mistakes: Using suspended for permanent removal; the American term for that is expelled or fired.
Saying 'suspended for school' instead of 'suspended from school'.

senses.definition: Fluid that exits the body through pores in the skin usually due to physical stress and/or high temperature for the purpose of regulating body temperature and removing certain compounds from the circulation.
senses.example: Sweat dripped from his forehead as he finished the marathon in ninety-degree heat.

senses.definition: The state of one who is sweating; diaphoresis.
senses.example: Just thinking about the interview tomorrow puts me into a nervous sweat.

senses.definition: Hard work; toil.
senses.example: Building the community garden took months of sweat from dedicated volunteers.

senses.definition: Moisture issuing from any substance.
senses.example: Cold sweat beaded on the outside of the lemonade glass.

senses.definition: A short run by a racehorse as a form of exercise.
senses.example: The trainer took the colt out for a light sweat before the Saturday race.

senses.definition: An extremely or excessively competitive player.
senses.example: In practice, Maria is a total sweat who never lets anyone rest.

senses.definition: (historical) The sweating sickness.
senses.example: The historian studied how the sweat swept through English towns in 1528.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To emit sweat.
senses.example: We began to sweat as soon as the air conditioner stopped working.

senses.definition: To cause to excrete moisture through skin.
senses.example: His physicians attempted to sweat him by most powerful sudorifics.

senses.definition: To cause to perspire.
senses.example: His physicians attempted to sweat him by most powerful sudorifics.

senses.definition: To work hard.
senses.example: I've been sweating over my essay all day.

senses.definition: To be extremely dedicated to winning a game; to play competitively.
senses.example: There's no way we can win. These guys are sweating so hard.

senses.definition: To extract money, labor, etc. from, by exaction or oppression.
senses.example: to sweat a spendthrift

senses.definition: To worry.
senses.example: Don't sweat it; the exam results will arrive next week anyway.

senses.definition: To worry about (something).
senses.example: Don't sweat it!

senses.definition: To emit, in the manner of sweat.
senses.example: to sweat blood

senses.definition: To emit moisture.
senses.example: The cheese will start sweating if you don't refrigerate it.

senses.definition: To have drops of water form on (something's surface) due to moisture condensation.
senses.example: Coasters are a good way to stop a sweating glass from damaging your table.

senses.definition: To solder (a pipe joint) together.
senses.example: My plumber had to sweat the copper joints before the water was turned back on.

senses.definition: To stress out, to put under pressure.
senses.example: Stop sweatin' me!

senses.definition: To cook slowly at low heat, in shallow oil and without browning, to reduce moisture content.
senses.example: Sweat the onions in olive oil until they turn translucent but not brown.

senses.definition: To suffer a penalty; to smart for one's misdeeds.
senses.example: The senator will sweat for those reckless comments once the press gets hold of them.

senses.definition: To take a racehorse for a short exercise run.
senses.example: Every morning the jockey sweats the filly on the training track before breakfast.

core.definition: Salty liquid that comes out through your skin, especially when you are hot, exercising or nervous, and helps cool your body.

pronunciation.tip: This is a one-syllable word with a short e, as in 'bet'. Do not add a vowel at the end, and do not say 'sweet', which has a long e and means something different.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for the body fluid. The word can sound negative when it describes unpleasant body odor or nervousness, and positive when it describes hard work or effort.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sweat often in everyday talk about weather, exercise and body temperature, such as 'I'm dripping with sweat.' The phrase 'no sweat' is a casual way to say 'no problem' or 'it's easy.' Using sweat in polite or formal writing, Americans may prefer perspiration, though sweat is still very common in speech.

distinctions.note: Perspiration is the more polite or medical word, often used in advertisements and formal writing, while sweat is the everyday word.
Toil means hard, tiring work, often over a long time, and is more formal or literary than sweat used in the sense of hard work.

examples.everyday: I'm dripping with sweat after that run, so I'm going to take a shower.
examples.professional: Don't sweat the small stuff in the deck; we can fix the chart labels before the client call.
examples.analytical: Aristotle's ideal of leisure assumes a life free from the sweat of daily labor, a life that the laborer rarely enjoys.

nuance.analogy: Sweat is the body's built-in air conditioner: it works by giving off moisture that cools the skin as it evaporates.
nuance.etymology: From Old English swāt, related to the idea of exuding moisture from the body.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I am sweat' instead of 'I am sweaty' or 'I am sweating'.
Confusing sweat with sweet, which is pronounced with a long e and means something tasting sugary.

sweat.etymology: From Middle English *swete*, *swet*, *swate*, *swote*, from Old English *swāt*, from Proto-Germanic **swait-*, from Proto-Indo-European **swoyd-* (“to sweat”), o-grade of **sweyd-* (“to sweat”).

senses.definition: Protuberant or abnormally distended (as by injury or disease).
senses.example: swollen ankle

core.definition: Enlarged or puffed up in size, usually from an injury, infection, illness, or fluid buildup.

pronunciation.tip: It has two syllables, with the stress on the first. Many learners add an extra syllable and say 'swo-LAN,' but the second syllable is short and reduced to a schwa.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative, because it usually describes a bodily or physical problem.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'My ankle is swollen' or 'My face is swollen from the allergy' in everyday conversation and at the doctor's office. The verb 'swell' is the root, and 'swelled' is also used as a past participle in casual speech. In medical contexts, 'edematous' is more technical.

distinctions.note: 'Swollen' is the adjective and past participle; 'swelled' is also common, especially in speech, as a past participle or past tense.
'Inflamed' describes redness, heat, and pain from inflammation, while 'swollen' describes size only.

examples.everyday: My ankle is still swollen from when I twisted it on the stairs.
examples.professional: The bug left the cache swollen, and memory usage kept climbing until the service crashed.
examples.analytical: A swollen estimate of variance, inflated by a few outliers, can make a real effect look statistically insignificant.

nuance.analogy: Like a balloon filled past its normal size, pushed out from the inside.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of Old English 'swellan', 'to swell.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'swo-LEN.'
Using 'swollen' as a verb in the past tense; the past tense of 'swell' is 'swelled,' and the past participle can be 'swollen' or 'swelled.'

swollen.etymology: From Middle English *swollen*, *i-swolle*, *y-swolle*, *yswolle*, *ȝeswollen*, from Old English *swollen*, *ġeswollen*, from Proto-Germanic **swullanaz*, past participle of Proto-Germanic **swellaną* (“to swell”).

conversation.text: My ankle is swollen from tripping on the stairs.
His face was swollen after the dentist.
Her eyes were red and swollen from crying.

senses.definition: One of a pair of red lights mounted on the rear of a vehicle, so it can be seen from the rear at night.
senses.example: A cracked taillight on his pickup made him pull over for a police officer.

core.definition: One of the red lights at the back of a vehicle that shows other drivers it is there, especially at night.

pronunciation.tip: Stress TAIL more than LIGHT, and keep both l sounds clear. The word sounds like 'tail' followed by 'lite', with the vowel of 'light' rhyming with 'bite'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, everyday word about cars.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say taillights for the pair, even when they mean both. A brake light is a separate, brighter light that comes on when you press the pedal, but many people use taillight loosely for both. If a light is broken, people say 'my taillight is out' and then take the car to a shop.

distinctions.note: A brake light is brighter and comes on only when the brakes are applied, while taillights stay on with the headlights.
Headlights face forward to light the road, while taillights face backward so that drivers behind can see you.

examples.everyday: Hey, your left taillight is out, so you should fix it before a police officer pulls you over.
examples.professional: The fleet inspection flagged three vans with a burned-out taillight, so we are scheduling replacements this week.
examples.analytical: Red taillights form a shared visual code that lets drivers read a car's presence and braking from behind in the dark.

nuance.analogy: A taillight works like a lighthouse facing backward, warning the traffic behind that you are there.
nuance.etymology: From tail, the rear part of something, plus light.
common_mistakes: Using taillight for the front lamps; the front ones are headlights.
Saying taillight in the singular when a car has two, as in 'the taillight is out' when both are dim; Americans often use the plural.

senses.definition: In a tame manner.

core.definition: In a meek, passive way, without resistance, anger, or spirit.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the vowel is the long 'ay' of 'tame', not a short 'a'. Don't add an extra syllable between the m and the l.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests a lack of spirit, courage, or resistance, as in giving in without a fight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tamely mostly in news, commentary, and sports writing, often to criticize someone who gave up too easily. In casual speech people more often say 'just gave up' or 'didn't put up a fight'. It is rarely used to describe an animal's calm behavior in everyday talk, where 'calmly' or 'quietly' is more natural.

distinctions.note: Meekly describes a humble, gentle character, while tamely emphasizes a failure to resist or fight back, often when resistance was expected.
Quietly is neutral and describes manner of speech or movement; tamely carries criticism of lost spirit.

examples.everyday: When the referee made that call, the other team just walked off the field tamely.
examples.professional: Our competitor accepted the new pricing rules tamely, so we lost our chance to negotiate better terms.
examples.analytical: Locke argues that a people who submit tamely to arbitrary power have forfeited the protection that government was meant to provide.

nuance.analogy: Like a dog that rolls over at the first command without a single growl, showing no fight at all.
nuance.etymology: From tame (Old English tam) plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first vowel as short, like 'tam-ly'; the vowel is the long 'ay' sound.
Using tamely to mean 'mildly' or 'gently' in neutral descriptions, when it usually implies a lack of spirit.

senses.definition: In a tangential manner or direction.
senses.example: The speaker touched only tangentially on the budget, focusing instead on staffing.

core.definition: Only slightly or indirectly related to the main topic, or in a side direction that touches the subject briefly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, JEN. The -tial is one syllable, 'shuh', and the ending is 'lee', so there are four syllables, not five.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a relationship between topics and carries no judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use tangentially in meetings, articles, and academic talk, usually in phrases like 'only tangentially related'. It is a polite way to say a point matters less. In casual speech people may say 'kind of related' or 'sort of off topic'.

distinctions.note: Indirectly means by a roundabout route; tangentially means only briefly touching the subject from the side.
Peripherally means at the edge of something; tangentially implies a brief point of contact with the main topic.

examples.everyday: That story about the trip is only tangentially related to what we're talking about, so let's get back to the plan.
examples.professional: The new metric is only tangentially relevant to our churn problem, so we'll put it in the appendix.
examples.analytical: Kant touches tangentially on the question of happiness, but he treats it as a matter of duty rather than of pleasure.

nuance.analogy: Like a ball that touches the edge of a circle once and then rolls off on its own path.
nuance.etymology: From tangential, from Latin tangere, to touch, with the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Adding an extra syllable, as in 'tan-gen-shee-ah-lee', instead of the four-syllable form.
Using it to mean 'in a tangent' as a physical movement, when it usually describes a topic or relationship.

senses.definition: An image made on a body part, usually the skin with ink and a needle.
senses.example: She got a small tattoo of a swallow on her wrist last summer.

senses.definition: A method of decorating a body part, usually the skin, by inserting colored substances under the surface with a sharp instrument (usually a solenoid-driven needle).
senses.example: The tattoo technique uses a needle that pushes pigment beneath the skin repeatedly.

senses.definition: A rhythmic tapping.
senses.example: The steady tattoo of rain on the tin roof kept me awake.

senses.definition: A pony of a certain breed from India.
senses.example: Our farm's little tattoo, a hardy Indian pony, pulls the children's cart every weekend.

senses.definition: A signal played five minutes before taps (lights out).
senses.example: At the base, the bugler played tattoo five minutes before taps sounded across the parade ground.

senses.definition: A signal by drum or bugle ordering soldiers to return to their quarters.
senses.example: When the drums sounded tattoo, the recruits hurried back to their barracks.

senses.definition: A military display or pageant.
senses.example: The city hosted a military tattoo with marching bands, horses, and fireworks.

senses.definition: To apply a tattoo to (someone or something).
senses.example: The artist tattooed a lighthouse across her shoulder blade in one long session.

senses.definition: To tap rhythmically on, to drum.
senses.example: He tattooed his fingers on the steering wheel while stuck in traffic.

senses.definition: To hit the ball hard, as if to figuratively leave a tattoo on the ball.
senses.example: Jones tattoos one into the gap in left; that will clear the bases.

core.definition: A permanent design made on the skin with ink and a needle.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable: 'ta-TOO.' The first vowel is the 'a' of 'cat,' not 'tah,' and many learners wrongly stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly informal; it can be personal, artistic, or rebellious depending on the design and the speaker.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'get a tattoo' and 'have a tattoo' in everyday speech, and people often ask 'Is that a tattoo?' about visible ink. Asking someone about their tattoo is generally fine, but do not ask about a placement that would be private. A natural reply is 'Yeah, I got it a few years ago,' or 'It means a lot to me.'

distinctions.note: Body art is a broader umbrella that includes piercings and scarification; tattoo is specifically ink in the skin.
A tattoo can also mean a rhythmic drumbeat or a military ceremony; context shows which meaning you mean.

examples.everyday: I finally got a tattoo of my dog's paw on my wrist.
examples.professional: The marketing team wants to avoid visible tattoos in the client-facing brand photos.
examples.analytical: Scholars of popular culture read the tattoo as a deliberate text written on the body.

nuance.analogy: A tattoo is like a signature in ink that the body keeps forever.
nuance.etymology: From Tahitian 'tatau,' an imitative word for striking, introduced to English through the accounts of Captain James Cook's voyages.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'TAT-oo' with stress on the first syllable.
Using 'tattoo' for a temporary sticker or henna, which Americans usually call a temporary tattoo or henna design.

tattoo.etymology: From earlier *tattaow*, *tattow*, a borrowing from a language, e.g.

senses.definition: The implied cost of additional future work caused by choosing an easy but inferior solution originally.
senses.example: Our team kept adding quick patches, and the technical debt slowed every new feature we shipped.

core.definition: The future cost of extra work created when a team chooses a quick, imperfect solution now instead of a better design.

pronunciation.tip: The word 'debt' is pronounced without the 'b', so say 'DET', not 'DEB-it'. The second word has the main stress, and 'technical' is pronounced with a weak final 'kuhl'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a problem that will cost time and money later.
nuance.usage_note: In American software teams, 'technical debt' is a common phrase in planning meetings, code reviews and engineering blogs. People say 'we're paying down technical debt' when they fix old shortcuts, and 'we're taking on technical debt' when they knowingly cut corners to meet a deadline. It is a metaphor, so it is informal, but professionals use it seriously.

distinctions.note: A bug is a specific error in the code, while technical debt is a broader design shortcut that makes future changes harder.
Refactoring is one way to repay technical debt by improving code structure without changing its behavior.

examples.everyday: My brother is a software developer, and he says their app is full of technical debt from rushed launches.
examples.professional: We need to allocate two sprints to reduce technical debt before adding the new payment feature.
examples.analytical: Ward Cunningham's metaphor treats quick shortcuts like borrowed money, which accrues interest in extra maintenance time.

nuance.analogy: Technical debt is like a credit card balance: you get the purchase now, but you pay interest every time you touch the system later.
nuance.etymology: Coined by software developer Ward Cunningham in the early 1990s, borrowing the financial term 'debt'.
common_mistakes: Treating 'technical debt' as countable, as in 'a technical debt'; it is usually uncountable, so say 'some technical debt'.
Confusing it with a bug; a bug is a single error, while technical debt is a structural shortcut.

senses.definition: A frequency or rate.
senses.example: 10 calls per hour isn't a bad start, but we'll need to up the tempo if we want to reach our target of selling insurance policies.

senses.definition: The timing advantage of being on lead, thus being first to initiate a strategy to develop tricks for one's side.
senses.example: Holding the lead gave our team the tempo to force the other side into early mistakes.

senses.definition: The timing of a particular event – earlier or later than in an alternative situation.
senses.example: the tempo effect in fertility measurements

senses.definition: The steady pace set by the frontmost riders.
senses.example: The breakaway riders set a brutal tempo that dropped most of the peloton.

senses.definition: A small truck or cargo van with three or four wheels, commonly used for commercial transport and deliveries (particularly in Asian and African countries).
senses.example: The tempo rattled down the dirt road, loaded with crates of vegetables for market.

senses.definition: A rapid rate of play by the offense resulting from reducing the amount of time which elapses after one play ends and the next starts.
senses.example: The offense ran a fast tempo, snapping the ball seconds after each whistle.

senses.definition: A temporary carport.
senses.example: We parked the car under a metal tempo beside the house during the storm.

senses.definition: A move which is part of one's own plan or strategy and forces, e.g. by means of a check or attacking a piece, the opponent to make a move which is not bad but of no use (the player gains a tempo, the opponent loses a tempo), or equivalently a player achieves the same result in fewer moves by one approach rather than another.
senses.example: Moving the bishop to attack his queen gained a tempo and forced his retreat.

senses.definition: The number of beats per minute in a piece of music; also, an indicative term denoting approximate rate of speed in written music (examples: allegro, andante)
senses.example: The conductor asked the orchestra to increase the tempo.

core.definition: The speed or pace at which something happens, such as a piece of music, a project or daily life.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the last vowel a long oh, like 'go'. Do not say 'TEM-pow' as in 'cow'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes pace and can be positive when a fast pace is desired.
nuance.usage_note: In American speech, tempo is most common in music and in phrases about the pace of work or life, such as 'the tempo of the meeting' or 'keep up the tempo.' It is slightly more formal than pace, which is the everyday word for how fast something is moving. The sports and game sense of tempo (for example, in bridge or basketball) is more specialized.

distinctions.note: Pace is the everyday word for speed of movement or progress, while tempo more often refers to a rhythm or a regular beat in music or a set schedule.
Rhythm refers to a pattern of sounds or events over time, while tempo is the speed at which that pattern is played or happens.

examples.everyday: The jazz band picked up the tempo halfway through, and the whole crowd started clapping faster.
examples.professional: We need to pick up the tempo on the migration, because the other teams are already waiting on our output.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that the tempo of modern life has changed how people experience time and memory.

nuance.analogy: Tempo is like the speed on a bicycle: the same route feels different depending on how fast you are pedaling.
nuance.etymology: From Italian tempo, time, from Latin tempus.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with an 'ow' vowel, as in 'TEM-pow'; the vowel is a long oh.
Using tempo as a plural form; the plural is tempi, but in everyday American speech people usually say tempos.

senses.definition: A specialty sports shoe designed for playing tennis.
A sneaker (trainer).

core.definition: A lightweight athletic shoe with a rubber sole, worn for sports or everyday walking; a sneaker.

pronunciation.tip: Tennis has two syllables in American speech, TEN-is, not three. The main stress falls on TEN, and shoe is a long 'oo' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and casual, with no strong emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say sneakers most often, but tennis shoes is also common, especially in the Midwest and South and among older speakers. A sneaker is a general term for casual athletic shoes, so tennis shoes is a clear way to say it. The British trainer would confuse most Americans, since the American word trainer usually means a coach or a fitness shoe.

distinctions.note: Sneaker is the most common American term for a casual athletic shoe, while tennis shoe stresses the original sport.
A running shoe is cushioned for forward motion, while a tennis shoe is built for side-to-side movement on a court.

examples.everyday: I'm wearing my old white tennis shoes to the gym, so my feet are going to be sore later.
examples.professional: Our warehouse policy allows tennis shoes on the floor, but not open-toed shoes.
examples.analytical: The tennis shoe's move from the court to the street shows how sport fashion reshaped everyday American dress.

nuance.analogy: A tennis shoe is the Swiss Army knife of footwear: built for one sport and used for almost everything.
nuance.etymology: Tennis from Old French tenez, hold!, shouted by players; shoe from Old English scoh.
common_mistakes: Saying TEN-uh-nis with three syllables, instead of TEN-is.
Using trainers, the British word, instead of sneakers or tennis shoes in American English.

senses.definition: Land that has never been explored, mapped, or surveyed.
senses.example: The expedition sailed past the coast into terra incognita, where no European map existed.

senses.definition: Ideas or concepts that have not yet been tried or explored.
senses.example: Our startup's plan for the AI product moved into terra incognita with no precedent.

core.definition: Unknown or unexplored territory, or an area of knowledge where no one has yet gone or mapped the way forward.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'NIH' in 'incognita,' with 'terra' lightly stressed. Americans often say 'in-kog-NEE-tuh' with a long e, but the General American form has a short i in the middle.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests adventure and discovery, but it can also suggest danger or the unknown.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this Latin phrase in writing, speeches, or academic talk, often humorously or to sound slightly literary. In casual speech, 'uncharted territory' is much more common. A natural reply to someone describing a new situation might be 'Yeah, we're in uncharted territory here.'

distinctions.note: 'Uncharted territory' is the everyday American English idiom with the same meaning and is more common in conversation.
'Incognito' means in disguise or with one's identity hidden; 'incognita' is a feminine Latin word meaning unknown, and the two should not be confused.

collocations: the terra incognita of machine learning

examples.everyday: Once we left the highway and drove into the mountains with no signal, it felt like terra incognita.
examples.professional: We are in terra incognita with this model, so let's run a small pilot before we commit to the full rollout.
examples.analytical: Kant's critique treats the limits of reason as a kind of terra incognita that the mind must map before it can trust its conclusions.

nuance.analogy: Like an old map with blank spaces and the warning 'here be dragons': the unknown part where no one has gone before.
nuance.etymology: Latin, literally 'unknown land,' from terra 'land' and incognita 'unknown.'
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'incognito,' which describes a person who is disguised or unidentified.
Using the masculine 'incognitus' or changing the ending; the phrase keeps the feminine 'incognita.'

senses.definition: To fill (someone) with terror; to terrify.
senses.example: terrorize the population

senses.definition: To coerce (someone) by using threats or violence.

core.definition: To fill someone with terror, or to control them through threats or violence.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, so the middle syllables are weak. The final -ize sounds like the ize in prize, and the American spelling is -ize, not -ise.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative; implies deliberate cruelty, bullying or abuse.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use terrorize for deliberate intimidation, whether by a gang, a bully or a government, and also loosely for something that frightens a person repeatedly, such as a noisy neighbor or a dog. It is stronger than scare, so in casual talk people often say scare or freak out instead. The American spelling is -ize, while British writers often use -ise.

distinctions.note: Scare is common and often lighter, while terrorize implies repeated or deliberate intimidation.
Intimidate means making someone afraid enough to change what they do; terrorize is stronger and often more violent.

examples.everyday: Those fireworks always terrorize our dog every July.
examples.professional: Anonymous trolls terrorized two maintainers of the project until they moved the discussion to private channels.
examples.analytical: Regimes that terrorize their citizens rely on fear as much as on force to keep order.

nuance.analogy: Like a storm that keeps coming back, terrorize describes a fear that never lets up.
nuance.etymology: From terror, with the verb-forming suffix -ize from Greek -izein.
common_mistakes: Spelling it terrorise, the British form; the American spelling is terrorize
Using terrorize for mild worry; it is too strong for a simple scare

senses.definition: A governor or ruler of a quarter of a country, especially of a fourth part of a province in or client state of Ancient Rome.
senses.example: The tetrarch of Galilee collected taxes from the towns along the lake.

senses.definition: Each of the four members of a jointly ruling tetrarchy, notably of the Roman Empire since Diocletian.
senses.example: Diocletian's reforms created a tetrarch system in which four rulers shared imperial power.

senses.definition: An officer in charge of a fourth part of a phalanx in Ancient Greece.
senses.example: The tetrarch shouted orders to the men of his section, holding the line at dawn.

senses.definition: Having four vascular strands in a fibrovascular cylinder or stele.
senses.example: The root cross-section showed a tetrarch stele with four distinct vascular strands.

core.definition: A ruler of a quarter of a province or territory under Roman rule, such as Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the final syllable a rhotic 'ark' sound. The 'ch' is silent, and the word ends with a hard k.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and historical, used in biblical studies and ancient history.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly meet 'tetrarch' in Bible classes, history courses, and religious studies. In everyday speech, people would simply say 'governor' or 'king' for a similar figure. The adjective form is used in botany for a plant structure, but this is rare outside science.

distinctions.note: A king rules a whole kingdom, while a tetrarch ruled only a quarter of a region, often under Roman authority.
An ethnarch ruled a people or ethnic group, while a tetrarch ruled a territorial division.

examples.everyday: In my Bible study, we read about Herod the tetrarch and how he ruled Galilee.
examples.professional: When we explain the Roman provinces to new staff, we mention that a tetrarch governed only a fraction of a region.
examples.analytical: Luke 3:1 identifies Herod as tetrarch of Galilee, a title that reflects the Roman division of Herod's inheritance.

nuance.analogy: A tetrarch is like a regional manager who runs one quarter of a larger company under the authority of the headquarters.
nuance.etymology: From Greek tetrarchēs, 'ruler of a fourth,' from tetra- 'four' and archein 'to rule.'
common_mistakes: Confusing 'tetrarch' with 'tetrarchy,' the system of four rulers, rather than the individual ruler.
Pronouncing the final 'ch' as in 'church'; the word ends with a k sound.
nuance.biblical_note: The title appears in the New Testament for Herod Antipas and his brother Philip. Luke 3:1 (RSV) names Herod as tetrarch of Galilee during John the Baptist's ministry. Matthew 14:1 says Herod the tetrarch heard about the fame of Jesus. Luke 23:6-12 describes Jesus before Herod, who was tetrarch of Galilee at the time.

tetrarch.etymology: Borrowed from Latin *tetrarchēs*, from Ancient Greek *τετράρχης*, from *τετρα-* (“four”) + *-άρχης* (“ruler, leader”).

senses.definition: In the manner of a theocrat.

core.definition: In a way that is governed by religious leaders who claim to rule in God's name.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on KRAT, the third syllable, and the first two syllables are quick and light. Don't stress the first syllable, and say the final -ly as a short 'lee' with a reduced vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in political science and history, but often critical in news and debate, where it suggests that religious authority overrides democratic or civil institutions.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in discussions of politics, history, or religion, such as describing Iran, medieval governments, or proposals to base law on scripture. Saying a country is governed theocratically is a claim about structure, not a comment on how devout its people are. In casual talk, people more often say the government is run by religious leaders.

distinctions.note: Theocratically describes how power is organized, while theologically describes how a question is reasoned about in terms of doctrine.
Religiously means devoutly or with regard to religious practice, while theocratically refers only to a political system in which clergy hold governing authority.

examples.everyday: A few religious leaders basically run that small town, so it's governed pretty theocratically.
examples.professional: The policy memo argues that the regime's courts operate theocratically, with clerics holding final authority over civil cases.
examples.analytical: Because the constitution places sovereign authority in the jurisprudent, the state can be described as governed theocratically in a formal sense.

nuance.analogy: If a democracy is a referee chosen by the players, a theocracy is a referee who claims to speak for the author of the rulebook.
nuance.etymology: From Greek theos 'god' and kratos 'rule'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with theologically, which concerns doctrine and reasoning rather than political rule.
Stressing the first syllable (THEE-uh-krat-ih-klee) instead of the KRAT syllable.

senses.definition: Someone who provides therapy, usually professionally.
senses.example: My therapist suggested I keep a journal to track my anxiety between our sessions.

senses.definition: A psychotherapist specifically.
senses.example: She sees a licensed therapist on Tuesdays to work through her childhood trauma.

core.definition: A trained professional who helps people with emotional, mental or physical problems through a structured treatment.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. The middle vowel is reduced to a quick uh, and the r is pronounced clearly in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it suggests professional help, though some people feel it means a serious problem.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say therapist for a licensed counselor, psychologist or social worker, and also for a physical therapist or speech therapist. People often say I see a therapist when talking about mental health care, which is common and not embarrassing. Use the specific title, such as physical therapist, if it is clear from the context.

distinctions.note: A counselor often helps with everyday life problems, while a therapist usually treats a diagnosed condition, though the terms overlap.
A psychiatrist is a medical doctor who can prescribe medication; a therapist usually cannot.

examples.everyday: My sister has been seeing a therapist every Tuesday since the move.
examples.professional: Our employee assistance program offers up to six free sessions with a licensed therapist.
examples.analytical: The therapist's role in this study is to deliver a standardized protocol, which makes outcomes easier to compare across sites.

nuance.analogy: A therapist is like a coach for the mind, guiding you through practice rather than doing the work for you.
nuance.etymology: From therapy plus the agent suffix -ist, one who practices therapy.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (thuh-RAP-ist).
Using therapist for a doctor who prescribes medicine; Americans would say psychiatrist for that.

conversation.text: Talking to a therapist really helped me during a tough year.
My physical therapist gave me some exercises for my shoulder.
She sees a therapist every other week.

senses.definition: The property of being thick (in dimension).
senses.example: The thickness of the drywall panel determines how well the wall blocks sound between rooms.

senses.definition: A measure of how thick (in dimension) something is.
senses.example: The thickness of the Earth's crust varies from two to 70 kilometres.

senses.definition: A layer.
senses.example: We upholstered the seat with three thicknesses of cloth to make it more comfortable to sit on.

senses.definition: The quality of being thick (in consistency).
senses.example: Whip the cream until it reaches a good thickness.

senses.definition: The property of being thick (slow to understand).
senses.example: Despite the obvious hints, his thickness kept him from realizing we were leaving the party early.

senses.definition: The minimum number of planar subgraphs which a given graph can decompose into.
senses.example: We proved that the thickness of this dense network graph is at least three, so it is not planar.

senses.definition: To trim (wood) to a consistent thickness using a thickness planer.
senses.example: The carpenter spent the morning thicknessing rough cherry boards to an even three-quarter inch.

core.definition: How thick something is, measured from one surface to its opposite; the distance between its two faces.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The -ness ending is a weak, unstressed vowel, so it sounds like 'nus,' not 'nes.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive. In manufacturing and construction it is precise and matter-of-fact.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'thickness' when measuring things, in construction specifications, and in cooking instructions such as 'roll the dough to a thickness of one-quarter inch.' In everyday talk people often say 'how thick is it?' instead. As a verb in woodworking, 'to thickness' a board means planing it to a consistent thickness.

distinctions.note: 'Depth' often refers to vertical or inward distance, like a hole; 'thickness' refers to the measurement across a flat object.
'Thickness' is the measurement or quality; a 'layer' is a single sheet or stratum that has a thickness.

examples.everyday: How much thickness do you want on the pizza crust, thin or regular?
examples.professional: The spec calls for a uniform thickness of three-quarters inch, so check the planer setting before you run the boards.
examples.analytical: The thickness of the argument matters less than its structure; a thin argument can still bear enormous philosophical weight.

nuance.analogy: Think of a stack of paper: the thickness is how tall the stack is, from the bottom sheet to the top.
nuance.etymology: From 'thick' plus the noun suffix '-ness,' meaning the state or quality of being thick.
common_mistakes: Saying 'thickness' for a person's weight; use 'heavyset' or 'build' instead.
Stressing the final syllable as 'thick-NESS' rather than 'THICK-ness.'

thickness.etymology: From Middle English *thikkenesse*, *thiknesse*, from Old English *þicnes* (“thickness, viscosity, density, hardness; obscurity, cloud, darkness; thicket; depth, a thick body, anything thick or heavy”), from **þikkwīnassī* (“thickness”), equivalent to…

senses.definition: The ordinal form of the number thirty-eight, describing a person or thing in position number 38 of a sequence.
senses.example: The answer appears on the thirty-eighth page of the book.

senses.definition: One of thirty-eight equal parts of a whole.
senses.example: A thirty-eighth of 760 is 20.

core.definition: Coming in position number 38 in a sequence, such as a date, order or rank.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on 'EIGHTH', and 'thirty' is pronounced with a weak second syllable 'tee'. The 'th' at the end is voiceless, as in 'eighth' and 'health'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is simply a counting or ordering term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ordinal numbers for dates, floors, anniversaries and editions, such as 'the thirty-eighth floor' or 'the thirty-eighth anniversary.' In speech, dates often say 'the thirty-eighth' when the day is the 38th, although the 38th day of a month is rare. Written ordinal forms like '38th' are common in print.

distinctions.note: Thirty-eight is a cardinal number meaning a quantity; thirty-eighth is an ordinal meaning a position.
Thirty-seventh is the position before the thirty-eighth; be careful not to swap them when counting or listing.

examples.everyday: We're on the thirty-eighth floor, so the elevator takes a while.
examples.professional: The thirty-eighth release of the library adds the new authentication module, so please update your dependencies.
examples.analytical: The thirty-eighth verse of the chapter shifts the argument from judgment to promise.

nuance.analogy: Like the thirty-eighth stair in a long staircase: you count past thirty-seven steps to reach it.
nuance.etymology: From 'thirty' (Old English thrittig) plus 'eighth' (Old English eahtoþa), forming a compound ordinal.
common_mistakes: Writing 'thirtyeighth' as one word; the standard form is 'thirty-eighth' with a hyphen.
Confusing the ordinal 'thirty-eighth' with the cardinal 'thirty-eight' when stating a quantity.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, thirty-eight appears as a period of time in Deuteronomy 2:14, which says the wandering in the wilderness lasted thirty-eight years. John 5:5 describes a man who had been ill for thirty-eight years and was healed by Jesus at the pool. These passages use the number to mark long spans of suffering and waiting.

senses.definition: A process, method, or way of thinking; a deliberate or planned course of reasoning in order to achieve a desired end; a thought process or train of thought.
senses.example: Her thought path moved from the data anomaly to a hypothesis about sensor drift.

core.definition: A planned sequence of reasoning steps moving from a starting point toward a goal or conclusion.

pronunciation.tip: Stress PATH, the second word, and keep 'thought' lighter. The th is voiceless, and the final th in 'path' is also voiceless, unlike the voiced th in 'the'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a descriptive phrase rather than a loaded term.
nuance.usage_note: 'Thought path' is less standard than 'train of thought' or 'line of reasoning', and you will mostly hear it in AI, design or cognitive-science discussions. In everyday American speech, say 'train of thought' or 'the way I was thinking about it.' In technical writing, 'chain of thought' is the more established term for step-by-step reasoning in language models.

distinctions.note: A train of thought is the flow of ideas as they occur to you; a thought path is more deliberately planned toward a specific end.
A line of reasoning is a formal argument you can state and defend; a thought path can be looser and more exploratory.
Chain of thought is a specific technical term for step-by-step reasoning in AI models; thought path is a general, less established phrase.

collocations: branch into a different thought path

examples.everyday: I lost my thought path halfway through explaining the plan, so let me start again.
examples.professional: The model should show its thought path so reviewers can see which assumptions led to the final recommendation.
examples.analytical: Her essay traces the thought path by which early modern thinkers moved from observation to general principle.

nuance.analogy: A thought path is like a trail through the woods: each step follows from the last, and the trail is easier to follow if it is marked.
nuance.etymology: A compound of 'thought' and 'path', from Old English pæþ.
common_mistakes: Using 'thought path' as if it were a fixed technical term in every field; 'line of reasoning' or 'train of thought' is often clearer.
Stressing 'thought' too strongly, which makes the phrase sound flat; the main stress falls on 'path'.

senses.definition: Showing thrift; economical; frugal.
senses.example: My thrifty roommate buys secondhand furniture and cooks big batches of rice every Sunday.

senses.definition: (dated) Thriving, prosperous, successful; growing rapidly or vigorously.
senses.example: Grandfather's shop was thrifty by the 1920s, with new customers arriving every single week.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: Careful with money; spending wisely and avoiding waste, so you save more and buy less that is unnecessary.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final 'y' is a clear 'ee' sound. Learners often stress the second syllable or pronounce the 'th' as a voiced sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive; calling someone thrifty is a compliment, although it can sound stingy if the person refuses to spend on necessities.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use thrifty to praise someone who saves money or buys sensibly, often in personal finance or family life. It is a friendly word in everyday speech. Be careful: calling someone cheap is insulting, while thrifty is respectful. The older sense, meaning thriving or prosperous, is rare today.

distinctions.note: Frugal sounds more formal and deliberate, often implying strict self-discipline, while thrifty is warmer and more everyday.
Cheap is negative and suggests unwillingness to spend, while thrifty is a compliment.
Economical describes things that use little money, fuel, or effort, while thrifty describes a person or habit.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is so thrifty that she fixes everything instead of buying new.
examples.professional: Our team is thrifty with cloud costs, so we shut down unused servers every Friday.
examples.analytical: The essay contrasts thrifty virtue with consumer excess, arguing that restraint can be a form of freedom.

nuance.analogy: A thrifty person is like a careful cook who uses every part of the chicken: nothing is thrown away, and every dollar works hard.
nuance.etymology: From thrift, plus the suffix -y.
common_mistakes: Using cheap as a compliment, when thrifty is the positive word.
Saying thrifty as a noun; the noun is thrift.

senses.definition: One who thunders.
senses.example: The old preacher was a thunderer who shook the rafters every Sunday.

core.definition: A person who speaks or shouts with loud, forceful, angry denunciation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllable is weak and the final -er is a reduced r-colored vowel, so do not stress the second or third syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative to neutral; it suggests bombastic, forceful or alarming speech.
nuance.usage_note: Thunderer is rare in American speech and mainly appears in literary, historical or religious writing. In everyday English you would say a loud, angry speaker, a ranter or a bully depending on context. The name the Thunderer is also used for the ancient god Zeus or Jupiter.

distinctions.note: An orator is a skilled public speaker, usually admired, while a thunderer is loud and denouncing rather than persuasive.
A ranter is an informal, everyday word for someone who complains loudly, while thunderer sounds more formal and dramatic.

examples.professional: The board chair was a thunderer in meetings, so people learned to speak carefully around him.
examples.analytical: The prophet appears in the narrative as a thunderer, whose words strike like weather rather than argument.

nuance.analogy: Like a summer storm that arrives suddenly and shakes the windows.
nuance.etymology: From thunder, from Old English thunor, plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Using thunderer for a person who literally makes thunder, which is not a normal meaning.
Using thunderer casually in everyday speech, where a more common word is clearer.
nuance.biblical_note: The word thunderer does not occur in Scripture. The closest biblical image is the nickname Boanerges, sons of thunder, given to James and John in Mark 3:17. The Greek word brontē, thunder, and the Hebrew ra'am describe God's voice as thunder, which shows the idea of a forceful speaker.

senses.definition: A malleable, ductile, metallic element, resistant to corrosion, with atomic number 50 and symbol Sn.
senses.example: Chemists know tin as a soft metal that resists corrosion and melts at low temperature.

senses.definition: Iron or steel sheet metal that is coated with tin as an anticorrosion protectant.
senses.example: The roof was made of tin, which had been cut with tin snips.

senses.definition: A metal pan used for baking, roasting, storing food, etc.
senses.example: muffin tin

senses.definition: The bottom part of the front wall, which is "out" if a player strikes it with the ball.
senses.example: His serve clipped the tin, and the rally ended immediately in favor of his opponent.

senses.definition: Computer hardware.
senses.example: The team spent more on tin than on software licenses this year.

senses.definition: (dated) Money, especially silver money.
senses.example: Old Harlan grumbled that he had no tin left to pay the ferryman.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: Made of tin.
senses.example: She drank her coffee from a tin cup at the campsite.

senses.definition: Made of galvanized iron or built of corrugated iron.
senses.example: The old barn still had a tin roof that rattled loudly in the wind.

senses.definition: Made of aluminum.
senses.example: She bought a tin baking pan that heats quickly.

senses.definition: To place into a metal can (ie. a tin; be it tin, steel, aluminum) in order to preserve.
senses.example: The farm family spent the late summer canning peaches and tinning tomatoes for winter.

senses.definition: To cover with tin.
senses.example: The roofers tinned the wooden gutters to protect them from rain.

senses.definition: To coat with solder.
senses.example: Before assembling the circuit, he tinned each copper wire end with solder.

senses.definition: To coat with solder, in preparation for soldering, to ensure a good solder joint.
senses.example: She tinned the iron tip so it would transfer heat cleanly.

senses.definition: To coat with solder, in order to consolidate braided wire, so as to make contact with all strands and reduce fragility of the fraying wire.
senses.example: He tinned the frayed braided wire so every strand held firm under the iron.

core.definition: A soft, silvery metal, chemical element Sn, used in alloys and to coat steel cans; also a metal container for food.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short, relaxed vowel like the 'i' in 'bit', so it rhymes with 'thin' and not with 'teen'. Avoid making it sound like 'teen'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a plain, practical word. The adjective tinny can sound negative, describing cheap or thin sound or quality.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, a food container is usually a can, so 'a can of soup' is standard. Tin is used for cookie tins, baking pans and the metal itself, as in 'a tin of cookies' or 'a tin roof'. Calling a soup can a tin would sound old-fashioned or British to most Americans.

distinctions.note: Can is the standard American word for a metal food container, usually steel or aluminum, while tin is more specific or older for that container.
Pewter is an alloy in which tin is the main ingredient, used for mugs and dishes, while tin is the pure metal.
Aluminum is lighter and cheaper and is the usual metal for soft-drink cans, while tin is heavier and resists corrosion well.

collocations: bronze, an alloy of copper and tin

examples.everyday: Can you grab that tin of cookies from the pantry for the kids?
examples.professional: The supplier said tin prices rose this quarter, so we should check our solder costs before the next order.
examples.analytical: Bronze, an alloy of copper and tin, shows how combining two metals can produce a material stronger than either one alone.

nuance.analogy: Tin is the quiet partner in bronze, lending its strength and coating to a metal that would otherwise rust or wear quickly.
nuance.etymology: From Old English tin, related to Dutch tin and German Zinn.
common_mistakes: Saying teen for tin, which changes the vowel and can cause confusion.
Calling a soup or vegetable can a tin in everyday American speech, where can is the normal word.

tin.etymology: From Middle English *tin*, from Old English *tin*, from **tin*, from Proto-Germanic **tiną*.

senses.definition: A simple harmonica.

core.definition: Slang for a harmonica, the small instrument played by blowing and drawing air through holes in a metal case.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on TIN, with a lighter stress on sand. The word is not a food here, so do not stress the second syllable of sandwich more than the first.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to playful; it is old-fashioned slang that suggests jazz or blues musicians.
nuance.usage_note: Tin sandwich is an old American slang term for a harmonica, mostly used by blues and folk players or in music history. Most Americans today just say harmonica. If you hear it, the context will make clear it is the instrument and not food.

distinctions.note: Harmonica is the standard name; tin sandwich is informal slang and sounds dated.
A kazoo changes a hummed voice into a buzzing sound through a membrane, while a tin sandwich is a reed instrument played with the mouth.

examples.everyday: My grandpa used to play a tin sandwich on the porch in the evenings, which is how I learned the word.
examples.professional: The music store's catalog lists the tin sandwich as a beginner's harmonica, so check the key before you order.
examples.analytical: Early blues musicians turned the cheap tin sandwich into a voice of its own, showing how humble objects can carry deep feeling.

nuance.analogy: Like calling a car a tin lizzie, the nickname describes the object's look and feel rather than its proper name.
nuance.etymology: American slang nickname; its exact origin is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Thinking it means an actual sandwich wrapped in tin; in this sense it means a harmonica.
Stressing sandwich equally with tin, which makes the phrase sound like two separate words.

senses.definition: A contribution to one's religious community or congregation of worship (notably to the LDS church).
senses.example: Every month the family pays their tithe to the church, as they have for decades.

senses.definition: A small part or proportion.
senses.example: Only a tithe of the donated funds went to the local food bank.

senses.definition: (historical) The tenth part of the increase arising from the profits of land and stock, allotted to the clergy for their support, as in England, or devoted to religious or charitable uses; a tax taking ten percent of land or stock profits, used for religious or charitable purposes.
senses.example: Medieval peasants were required to give a tithe of their harvest to the parish priest.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To give one-tenth or a tithe of something, particularly:
senses.example: My grandmother insisted that we tithe our paychecks, giving the first ten percent to charity.

senses.definition: To pay something as a tithe.
senses.example: Our church asks members to tithe their income each year to fund its youth programs.

senses.definition: To pay a tithe upon something.
senses.example: Many small business owners tithe on their profits before paying themselves a salary.

senses.definition: To pay a tithe; to pay a 10% tax.
senses.example: Under the old system, farmers had to tithe to the crown.

senses.definition: To pay or offer as a levy in the manner of a tithe or religious tax.
senses.example: The merchants agreed to tithe a portion of their earnings toward the new bridge fund.

senses.definition: To take one-tenth or a tithe of something, particularly:
senses.example: The clerk was ordered to tithe the grain stores for the royal treasury.

senses.definition: To impose a tithe upon someone or something.
senses.example: The lord decided to tithe every village in the valley to fund the new castle.

senses.definition: To spare only every tenth person, killing the rest.
senses.example: The general ordered his soldiers to tithe the mutinous regiment, executing every tenth man.

senses.definition: To enforce or collect a tithe upon someone or something.
senses.example: The abbey's agents rode out each autumn to tithe throughout the district.

senses.definition: To enforce or collect a tithe.
senses.example: The abbey's agents rode out each autumn to tithe throughout the district.

core.definition: One tenth of a person's income, given to a church or religious community; also, to give such a tenth.

pronunciation.tip: One syllable, rhymes with 'scythe' and 'writhe'. The final th is voiced, as in 'breathe', not the voiceless th of 'tooth'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive among believers, as faithful giving; some people see it as an obligation or pressure, depending on the church.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'tithe' mostly in church settings, as both noun and verb ('We tithe ten percent'). Many evangelical, Mormon and other churches teach it. Outside religion it is rare, and the sense 'a small part' is archaic.

distinctions.note: An offering is any gift to God or the church; a tithe is specifically one tenth.
A donation is a general gift to any cause and has no fixed amount; a tithe is religious and fixed at a tenth.
A tax is compulsory and civil; a tithe was historically a church tax but is now usually voluntary.

examples.everyday: My family has tithed every month since I was a kid.
examples.professional: The church's budget depends largely on members' tithes and offerings.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate whether the Mosaic tithe binds Christians or was fulfilled in the new covenant.

nuance.analogy: A tithe is like a tenth slice of every pie you bake, set aside before you serve the rest.
nuance.etymology: From Old English teogoþa, 'tenth', related to ten.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the th as voiceless /θ/ like 'tooth'; it is voiced /ð/.
Treating it as a general word for any donation.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew ma'aser means 'a tenth'. Genesis 14:20 says Abraham gave Melchizedek a tenth of everything. Leviticus 27:30 says the tithe of the land belongs to the LORD. Malachi 3:10 urges bringing the full tithe into the storehouse. In the New Testament, Matthew 23:23 has Jesus criticize tithing small herbs while neglecting justice and mercy.

traditions.view: Giving a portion of income is encouraged as stewardship and almsgiving, but there is no universal binding rule of ten percent. Practice varies by jurisdiction and parish.
The Church requires believers to support its needs, but the old ten-percent tithe is not a fixed obligation. Many Catholics treat it as a guideline for generosity.

Many evangelical, Baptist and Pentecostal churches teach tithing as a standard of giving. Others, including some Lutheran and Reformed teachers, see it as a helpful guide rather than a binding law, stressing cheerful and proportionate giving.

tithe.etymology: From Middle English *tithe*, *tythe*, *tethe*, from Old English *tēoþa*, *tēoða*, *teogoþa* (in verb senses via Middle English *tithen*, *tythen*, *tethen*, from Old English *tēoþian*, *teogoþian*), from a proposed Proto-Germanic **tehunþô*, **tehundô* (“a…

core.definition: The son of Tobit in the Book of Tobit, who travels with the angel Raphael, disguised as a man named Azarias, and returns with a bride and a cure for his father's blindness.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, BY, and the final -ias is pronounced like 'uhs', with a reduced vowel. Americans often say the middle as 'by-uh', not 'bee-uh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Tobias is a name you hear mostly in religious or literary contexts, and as a given name for people in the United States. Outside of Bible study it is not a common word, so learners mainly need it to follow a conversation about Scripture or a Catholic or Orthodox reading list.

distinctions.note: Tobit is the father and main figure of the book; Tobias is the son who undertakes the journey.

examples.everyday: My friend named her son Tobias after a character in an old Bible story.
examples.professional: In my seminar paper I compare how Tobias is portrayed as a young man learning to trust God on the road.
examples.analytical: The narrative of Tobias shows filial duty and divine guidance working together, as the young man's obedience to his father opens the way for Raphael's protection.

nuance.analogy: Tobias is like a young apprentice who goes on a dangerous errand with a guide he does not yet recognize.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Tobiyah, meaning 'Yahweh is good'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'toh-BYE-us' with a long final vowel instead of the reduced 'uhs' ending.
Stressing the first syllable, as in 'TOH-bee-us'.
nuance.biblical_note: Tobias is the son of Tobit in the book of Tobit, which appears in the Apocrypha in the RSV. He travels to Media with the angel Raphael, who is disguised as Azarias, and fulfills his father's request to recover money deposited there. Tobit 5:4-16 describes the departure with Raphael as guide. Tobit 6:1-9 tells of the fish whose heart and liver drive off a demon, and Tobit 8:2-3 describes Tobias's marriage to Sarah and the defeat of Asmodeus. Tobit 11:7-13 describes the healing of Tobit's eyes.

core.definition: A judge of Israel from the tribe of Issachar who led the nation for twenty-three years, named in the Book of Judges.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second syllable is a reduced schwa, so say 'luh', not 'lah'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is simply a name or a historical reference.
nuance.usage_note: Tola is used as a personal name in English-speaking communities and as a biblical name. Americans who know the Bible might recognize it from Judges, but most people will not. It is not commonly used as a common noun.

examples.everyday: My neighbor's son is named Tola, after a judge in the Bible.
examples.professional: In the lesson, the teacher explained that Tola judged Israel after Abimelech and before Jair.
examples.analytical: Judges 10:1-2 gives Tola only a brief record, which contrasts with the fuller accounts of Gideon and Jephthah.

nuance.analogy: Like a short entry in a long list of names in a historical chronicle.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew tola', meaning 'worm' or 'crimson'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the second syllable as 'lah', as in 'TOH-lah'.
Confusing Tola with Tolar or Toll, which are unrelated words.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew the name is Tola' (tolaʿ), meaning 'worm' or 'crimson', a term also linked to scarlet dye. Tola appears as a son of Issachar in Genesis 46:13 and 1 Chronicles 7:1-2, where he is listed among the tribe's heads. In Judges 10:1-2 he is said to have arisen to save Israel and to have judged it for twenty-three years, living at Shamir in the hill country of Ephraim.

senses.definition: In a tolerant manner.
With tolerance.
senses.example: My daughter's teacher listened tolerantly to every wild theory about the solar system.

core.definition: In a patient, accepting way, without strongly disapproving of what others say, believe, or do.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, TOL, and the middle syllables are weak, so their vowels reduce to a schwa. Keep the r light and do not stress the final -ly.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes fair acceptance of differences, though it can sound distant if used of someone who merely ignores something.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it mostly in writing and in discussions of social issues, such as how a school or city treats people with different views. In everyday speech people more often say they took something well or were understanding. Applied to someone who grudgingly puts up with something, it can suggest reluctance, so patiently or calmly may fit better.

distinctions.note: Patiently stresses waiting calmly without complaint, while tolerantly stresses accepting views or behavior one might dislike.
Indulgently means being excessively lenient, often spoiling someone, whereas tolerantly implies fairness without overindulgence.

examples.everyday: My neighbor doesn't mind our dog barking in the yard, and she handles our noisy parties pretty tolerantly.
examples.professional: In the review meeting, Dana listened tolerantly to the junior analysts' objections and answered each one patiently.
examples.analytical: A liberal state may govern tolerantly, extending equal protection to citizens whose convictions it does not share.

nuance.analogy: Like a thick-skinned referee who lets players argue the call without stopping the game.
nuance.etymology: From Latin tolerare, to bear or endure, plus the suffixes -ant and -ly.
common_mistakes: Saying tolerantly when you mean tolerably, which means fairly well or adequately, as in 'The soup was tolerably good.'

senses.definition: A tote bag.
senses.example: She slung her canvas tote over her shoulder and headed out to the farmers market.

senses.definition: A heavy burden.
senses.example: Managing the family finances had become a heavy tote she could no longer bear alone.

senses.definition: A kind of plastic box used for transporting goods.
senses.example: We stacked the plastic totes in the garage, each labeled with the holiday decorations inside.

senses.definition: The principal handle of a handplane, for gripping the plane.
senses.example: Grip the tote firmly with your right hand while you push the plane across the board.

senses.definition: To carry or bear.
To add up; to calculate a total.
senses.example: Please tote up the receipts so we know exactly what the project cost.

core.definition: To carry something heavy or bulky, usually with your hands or over your shoulder, from one place to another.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a glide from oh to oo, ending in a crisp t. Don't let it drift into 'toot' or 'tote' with a short o.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes ordinary carrying and can sound a little folksy or casual.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'tote' as an informal verb for carrying bags, boxes or gear, as in 'toting groceries' or 'toting a laptop around all day.' The noun 'tote bag' is far more common than the verb in everyday speech. Saying 'tote' in a formal report would sound too casual, so use 'carry' or 'transport' there.

distinctions.note: Carry is the general, neutral word for holding something and moving it, while tote suggests carrying something bulky or heavy.
Lug stresses the physical effort of dragging or hauling something awkward, often with more strain than tote implies.

examples.everyday: I'm toting these grocery bags from the car, so can you grab the door?
examples.professional: I had to tote the sample cases from the lab to the conference room myself.
examples.analytical: The essay notes that the workers toted the heavy equipment across the site without any mechanical support.

nuance.analogy: Like a camel carrying a load across the desert, steady and burdened.
nuance.etymology: Of uncertain origin, possibly from an Algonquian language of Virginia.
common_mistakes: Saying 'tote' for a small purse; a tote is usually large and open at the top.
Pronouncing it like 'toot' with a short vowel.

senses.definition: In the direction of.
senses.example: She moved toward the door.

senses.definition: In relation to (someone or something).
senses.example: What are your feelings toward him?

senses.definition: For the purpose of attaining (an aim).
senses.example: I'm saving money toward retirement.

senses.definition: Located close to; near (a time or place).
senses.example: Our place is over toward the station.

senses.definition: Yielding, pliant; docile; ready or apt to learn; not froward.
senses.example: The shepherd preferred a dog that was toward and quick to learn commands.

senses.definition: (rare) Happening; going on.
senses.example: Something toward was going on in the back office, and nobody would say what.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: In the direction of someone or something; moving closer to a place, person or goal.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a strong r and the vowel of 'thaw' or 'caught'. Some speakers use a weak first syllable, /təˈwɔɹd/, which is also acceptable, but avoid two strong beats.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a plain, everyday preposition.
nuance.usage_note: Americans prefer 'toward' to 'towards', which is more common in British English. Use it for direction or progress, as in 'walking toward the door' or 'progress toward a goal'. The older adjective senses, such as 'yielding' or 'docile', are archaic and rarely used today.

distinctions.note: 'To' describes reaching a destination, while 'toward' describes moving in its direction without necessarily arriving.
'Towards' is the more common form in British English; Americans usually write 'toward'.

examples.everyday: We are heading toward the lake now, so we should get there before sunset.
examples.professional: The team is making steady progress toward the Q3 launch, despite the delays.
examples.analytical: Her argument moves toward a conclusion that the evidence itself does not fully support.

nuance.analogy: Toward is like the needle on a compass: it shows the direction you face, not whether you have arrived.
nuance.etymology: From Old English tōweard, from tō ('to') and -weard ('-ward').
common_mistakes: Using 'toward' for arrival, as in 'I walked toward school' when you got there; use 'to school'.
Writing 'towards' in American formal writing, where 'toward' is standard.
Saying it as two stressed syllables, 'TOH-word'.

toward.etymology: From Middle English *toward*, from Old English *tōweard*, from **tōward*, equivalent to *to* + *ward*.

senses.definition: A house in an urban setting.
senses.example: They bought a narrow townhouse in Brooklyn with a tiny garden out back.

senses.definition: (dated) A town hall.
senses.example: The townhouse was where the councilmen met every Tuesday to argue about zoning.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: A house joined to one or more neighboring houses by shared walls, usually in a city or suburb.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'town', and the 'ow' in both syllables is the same diphthong. In the second syllable, 'house' is pronounced 'hows', not 'hoos'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests urban living, modern design, and a home with some private outdoor space.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'townhouse' for a multi-story house joined to its neighbors, common in cities and new developments. The British word is 'terraced house' or 'terrace house', so Americans would not use that term. A typical comment is 'We bought a townhouse near the park,' and a natural reply is 'How many bedrooms does it have?'

distinctions.note: A 'condo' is a unit in a building that you own, while a 'townhouse' is usually a whole house, often with its own entrance and yard.
A 'duplex' is a single building with two separate units, while a 'townhouse' is one of a row of attached houses.

examples.everyday: We moved into a townhouse last year, so we finally have a small patio for grilling.
examples.professional: The developer is adding forty townhouse units to the east lot, and the HOA has approved the new design.
examples.analytical: The townhouse form reconciles density with private outdoor space, though it often transfers maintenance responsibility to a shared association.

nuance.analogy: A townhouse is like a row of books on a shelf: each one is separate, but they lean against each other and share the same support.
nuance.etymology: Combines 'town' and 'house', recorded in English from the 17th century for a house in a town.
common_mistakes: Using 'townhouse' for a town hall, which is a government building.
Saying 'terrace house' in American conversation, which sounds British.

conversation.text: We live in a townhouse, so we share walls with our neighbors.
The townhouse has three floors and a small backyard.
Townhouses here are cheaper than single-family homes.

senses.definition: Agent noun of track; one who, or that which, tracks or pursues, as a man or dog that follows game.
senses.example: The hunter hired a tracker to follow the wounded deer across the ridge.

senses.definition: A person employed to follow and monitor a political rival.
An Indigenous Australian employed by the law to track down fugitives and missing persons.
senses.example: The police called an Indigenous Australian tracker to search the desert for the fugitive.

senses.definition: In an organ, a light strip of wood connecting (in path) a key and a pallet, to communicate motion by pulling.
senses.example: The organist checked each tracker to make sure the pallets moved freely.

senses.definition: A type of computer software for composing music by aligning notes or samples on parallel timelines.
senses.example: She composed the drum pattern in a tracker, lining up samples on parallel timelines.

senses.definition: A musician who writes music in a tracker.
senses.example: The chiptune musician is a respected tracker who writes albums on old software.

senses.definition: A computer program that monitors something.
Server software that coordinates peers in the BitTorrent protocol.
senses.example: Our university network blocks the tracker that coordinates peers for large downloads.

senses.definition: A tracker mortgage.
senses.example: They refinanced into a tracker mortgage that follows the central bank rate.

senses.definition: An album with the specified number of tracks.
senses.example: The band's new fourteen-tracker album arrived on streaming services this morning.

core.definition: A person or device that follows, monitors or records the movement or progress of someone or something over time.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, TRAK. The final syllable is weak and r-colored, like 'er' in 'butter', not 'ah'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses; can sound invasive when applied to people, as in a tracker that follows someone's location.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'tracker' most often for devices such as a fitness tracker, a GPS tracker or a package tracker. In software, a bug tracker is a tool where teams log and follow problems. In Australia, 'tracker' also refers to an Aboriginal guide who follows trails, a meaning that is rare in American English.

distinctions.note: A tracer is a substance or signal added to a system to follow its flow; a tracker follows a person, animal or object.
A monitor watches something continuously against a standard; a tracker follows where something goes or how it progresses.

examples.everyday: My fitness tracker says I walked about eight thousand steps today.
examples.professional: Please log the bug in the issue tracker so the team can prioritize it for next sprint.
examples.analytical: A good tracker reasons from partial traces toward a conclusion, much as historians reconstruct the past from incomplete evidence.

nuance.analogy: A GPS tracker is like a flight board at an airport that keeps updating where each plane is.
nuance.etymology: From the verb track plus the agent suffix -er, meaning one who tracks.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'tra-KER'.
Using 'tracker' for a person who follows a path when Americans would say 'scout' or 'guide' in ordinary talk.

senses.definition: Not culturally specific.
Extending through more than one human culture.
senses.example: The festival's transcultural program brought together music from Nigeria, Brazil, and Vietnam.

core.definition: Involving or spanning several cultures, or applying across cultures rather than belonging to one specific culture.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KUL, the second syllable, and the -ural ending reduces to 'chur-ul'. The first syllable sounds like 'trans' in trance, not 'trains'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive, suggesting openness and shared human experience.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in academic fields like anthropology, psychiatry, design and business to describe ideas or practices that cross cultural lines. In everyday talk they more often say cross-cultural or multicultural. Some scholars dispute whether anything can be fully transcultural, so the word can sound claim-heavy.

distinctions.note: Compares or involves two or more cultures, and is often about differences between them.
Focuses on interaction and exchange between cultures, such as intercultural communication.
Describes a place or group where several cultures exist side by side, such as a multicultural city.

examples.everyday: Her cooking is transcultural, with Mexican flavors and Japanese technique, and somehow it all works.
examples.professional: Our onboarding materials need transcultural design so they work for teams in Manila and Chicago alike.
examples.analytical: Some ethical principles are presented as transcultural, yet their justifications often rest on categories drawn from a single tradition.

nuance.analogy: A melody that listeners recognize even when it is played on different instruments in different countries.
nuance.etymology: Trans-, meaning across, plus culture, from Latin cultura.
common_mistakes: Treating it as a synonym for multicultural, when it means not tied to one culture.
Stressing the first syllable as TRANS-kul-chur-ul instead of trans-KUL-chur-ul.

senses.definition: Someone who transfers his property to another.

core.definition: A person who transfers property, a right or ownership to another person.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on FUR, and the final -or is pronounced 'er', the same unstressed ending you hear in 'teacher'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise legal or financial term without emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use transferor mainly in legal, financial and real estate documents, where the transferor and transferee are named parties. In everyday speech they'd say the person selling it or the one giving it away. Don't use transferor for an employee who moves; that person is a transferee.

distinctions.note: A transferor gives or conveys the property, rights or ownership, while a transferee receives them.
Grantor is a narrower legal term for someone who conveys real estate by deed; transferor covers any kind of transfer.
